Lesson 01 -- Pre-class

Who Is Caio, in English? -- The Founder in the Room

A stranger at a conference asks what your company does, and the answer has to fit three sentences. Key words: founder, to specialize in, revenue, stakeholder, deal, negotiation, expansion, acquisition, consulting, to be responsible for. Structure: the third-person singular -s in the present simple.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A founder -- the person who started the company and still owns part of it
"I am the founder of Dataside, and I have run it for fifteen years."
To specialize in -- to do one thing extremely well, and only that thing
"We specialize in data and artificial intelligence."
Revenue -- the money a business brings in before any costs are taken out
"Most of our revenue comes from long consulting contracts."
A stakeholder -- anyone whose money or decisions are tied to the result
"Every stakeholder in this deal wants to see the same numbers."
A deal -- the agreement two companies sign when the negotiation is finished
"We lost a deal worth a hundred and ten million reais."
A negotiation -- the conversation where each side moves until the terms fit both
"The negotiation took nine months and four meetings in New York."
Expansion -- opening the business in a new country or a new market
"Expansion into the United States is the reason I am learning English."
An acquisition -- the purchase of one company by another
"An acquisition is not only about price. It is about trust."
Consulting -- selling expert work by the project or by the hour, not a product
"Consulting means our people work inside the client company."
To be responsible for -- to own the result, and to answer for it in front of other people
"I am responsible for every number in this presentation."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

A buyer in New York asks a founder what his company does, and the founder answers well — the numbers are right, the story is clear, the strategy holds. And still, something in the room moves half a step back. Later nobody can say exactly what it was. It was one letter. Dataside specialize in data, he said. The buyer want a faster close. Three or four times in ten minutes, and each time the sentence arrived a little less finished than the thought behind it.

English marks one person in the present simple, and only one. When the subject is he, she or it, the verb carries an -s: she wants, he runs, it costs. Everybody else takes the bare verb: I run, we specialize, they want. The trap for a Portuguese speaker is not the rule — the rule is simple and most speakers can recite it. The trap is the subject that does not look like a person. Dataside has three hundred people, because a company is an it. Revenue comes from consulting, because revenue is an it too. The private equity firm wants three years of numbers. Every one of those subjects is a single thing, and every one of them takes the -s.

In the negative and in questions the -s moves house. It leaves the main verb and goes to do: he does not move on price, and does the buyer need more time? Saying she does not wants puts it in both places, which is the second most common version of the same mistake. And there is a habit that travels from Portuguese with it: depends of instead of it depends on. Neither one changes what a founder means. Both change how finished the founder sounds, and in a first meeting that is the only thing a buyer has to go on.

Explicação em portuguêsPresent simple e o -s da terceira pessoaToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. É o tempo verbal do que é verdade sempre, do que a empresa faz e de como as coisas funcionam: “We specialize in data” (a gente é especialista em dados), “Revenue comes from consulting” (a receita vem de consultoria). Em português o verbo muda para cada pessoa (eu faço, ele faz, nós fazemos). Em inglês ele quase não muda: a única mudança é um -s quando o sujeito é he, she ou it.

2. Quando usar. Para apresentar a Dataside, explicar o que vocês fazem, de onde vem o dinheiro e como o comprador trabalha. É o tempo da primeira reunião. E é onde o -s faltando mais aparece, porque você fala da empresa o tempo todo.

3. A regra em uma frase. Sujeito he, she, it (ou qualquer coisa que seja uma só: uma empresa, a receita, o comprador) leva -s no verbo. Todo o resto fica sem nada.

4. Quem leva -s e quem não leva

SujeitoVerboExemploEm português
I, you, we, theysem nadaWe specialize in data and AI.A gente é especialista em dados e IA.
he, she, itcom -sShe wants a faster close.Ela quer fechar mais rápido.
uma empresa (= it)com -sDataside specializes in data.A Dataside é especialista em dados.
uma coisa (= it)com -sMost of our revenue comes from consulting.A maior parte da nossa receita vem de consultoria.
uma pessoa (= he / she)com -sThe buyer wants three years of numbers.O comprador quer três anos de números.
várias pessoas (= they)sem nadaOur engineers work inside the client company.Nossos engenheiros trabalham dentro da empresa do cliente.

O truque: antes de falar, pergunte “o sujeito é uma coisa só?”. Se for, o verbo leva -s. Dataside, revenue, the firm, the market: tudo isso é it.

5. Como escrever o -s

Quase sempre é só acrescentar -s: work → works, want → wants, run → runs.

Termina em -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: acrescenta -es. focus → focuses, finish → finishes, go → goes, do → does.

Termina em consoante + y: troca por -ies. specify → specifies, try → tries.

Irregular: have → has. Dataside has three hundred people. (A Dataside tem trezentas pessoas.)

6. Na negativa e na pergunta, o -s muda de lugar

TipoComo ficaExemploEm português
Afirmativaverbo + -sHe moves on price.Ele cede no preço.
Negativadoes not + verbo sem nadaThe buyer does not move on price.O comprador não cede no preço.
PerguntaDoes + sujeito + verbo sem nadaDoes the buyer need more time?O comprador precisa de mais tempo?
Com I / we / theydo not / DoWe do not sell software. Do they want the data?A gente não vende software. Eles querem os dados?

O -s vai para o does e sai do verbo principal. Nunca nos dois lugares ao mesmo tempo.

7. Onde o português atrapalha

A empresa não parece uma pessoa. Em português “a Dataside é especialista” soa natural e você não pensa em pessoa nenhuma. Em inglês a empresa é um it, então leva -s igual a he e she.

Depender DE vira depender ON. Em português é “depende de”. Em inglês é it depends on. It depends on the valuation. (Depende do valuation.)

8. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Em vez deDigaPor quê
Dataside specialize in dataDataside specializes in dataEmpresa é it: leva -s.
The buyer want a faster closeThe buyer wants a faster closeO comprador é uma pessoa só.
She does not wantsShe does not wantO -s já está no does.
Does he needs more time?Does he need more time?Mesma coisa na pergunta.
It depends of the valuationIt depends on the valuationEm inglês é on.

EM PORTUGUÊS

(o comprador precisa de mais tempo?). Dizer she does not wants coloca o -s nos dois lugares, que é a segunda versão mais comum do mesmo erro.

And there is a habit that travels from Portuguese with it: depends of instead of it depends on. Neither one changes what a founder means. Both change how finished the founder sounds, and in a first meeting that is the only thing a buyer has to go on.

E tem um hábito que vem do português junto: depends of em vez de it depends on. Nenhum dos dois muda o que o fundador quer dizer. Os dois mudam o quanto ele soa acabado, e numa primeira reunião essa é a única coisa que o comprador tem para avaliar.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- The Third-Person Singular -S

GRAMMAR

One letter. It decides whether the sentence sounds finished.

JobFormExample
I / you / we / theybare verbWe specialize in data.
he / she / itverb + -sShe wants a faster close.
the company, the buyer, the marketcounts as it → verb + -sDataside has three hundred people.
two or more people or thingsbare verbOur engineers work inside the client company.
negative, he / she / itdoes not + bare verbHe does not move on price.
question, he / she / itdoes + subject + bare verbDoes the buyer need more time?
the trapthe -s goes on does, never on bothNot she doesn't wants. Say she doesn't want.

Never: She like the proposal · Our company have three hundred people · The buyer want a faster close · Depends of the valuation

Lesson 02 -- Pre-class

Fifteen Years in Four Paragraphs -- The Company History a Buyer Reads

A founder took nine years to learn the one sentence that explains her company. Key words: a consultancy, AI-driven, scalable, a track record, a milestone, a portfolio, headquartered, to scale up. Structure: the present perfect for company history.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A consultancy -- a firm that sells expert people and their time, not a product
"Vantia is a consultancy of a hundred and forty people."
AI-driven -- built so that the decisions are made by a model, not by a person
"We have delivered AI-driven forecasting for eleven banks."
Scalable -- able to grow a lot without costing proportionally more to run
"Consulting is profitable, but it is not scalable the way software is."
A track record -- everything you have already delivered, used as proof that you can do it again
"A track record is the one argument a buyer cannot argue with."
A milestone -- a point in the company's history big enough to be worth naming
"Our last milestone was the two-hundredth project."
A portfolio -- the full set of products, clients or projects a company holds
"Our portfolio has grown from eight clients to a hundred and eighty."
Headquartered -- having its main office in a particular city
"We are headquartered in Sao Jose dos Campos."
To scale up -- to make the business much bigger without rebuilding it from zero
"We have spent two years learning how to scale up."

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

There is a moment in every first meeting when a buyer stops asking what the company does and starts asking what it has done. The two questions sound similar and they are not. The first one can be answered by anybody with a website. The second one can only be answered by a company with a history, and English keeps a separate shape for it. Dataside has been operating for fifteen years. We have delivered more than four hundred projects. We have never lost a client to a competitor. None of those three sentences carries a date, and that is the whole point.

The shape is have or has plus the past participle, and it does one job: it says the count is still running. Four hundred projects today, four hundred and one next month. Compare that with we opened our second office in 2018. The year is named, the sentence closes, and nothing about it can change. That is the past simple, and it is the right shape whenever the time is on the table. The rule underneath both is short enough to carry into a meeting: name the time and the sentence closes; leave the time out and you are still counting. With for and since the count is explicit — for takes a length of time, since takes a starting point — and both of them require the present perfect, always.

Two traps cost a Portuguese speaker the most, and they are both traps of translation rather than of grammar. The first is since with the simple present. In Portuguese the equivalent sentence sits comfortably in the present tense, so the direct translation arrives as I am CEO since 2009. English will not take it: it has to be I have been CEO since 2009. The second trap is a named time glued to a present perfect — Last year we have opened an office — and the fix is to drop back to the past simple: Last year we opened an office. And underneath both, the permanent one: a company is an it, so it takes has. Not Dataside have grown. Dataside has grown.

Explicação em portuguêsPresent perfect x past simple, com for e sinceToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. São dois jeitos de falar do passado. O past simple (we opened) conta um fato com data, que já fechou. O present perfect (we have opened) fala de algo que começou no passado e ainda conta hoje, sem dizer quando. Em português a gente usa o mesmo “abrimos” para as duas coisas; em inglês são duas formas diferentes.

2. Quando usar. Quando o comprador pergunta o que a empresa já fez: histórico, número de projetos, há quanto tempo vocês existem. Tudo o que é “até hoje” vai para o present perfect. Tudo o que tem ano, mês ou “last year” vai para o past simple.

3. A regra em uma frase. Disse quando, a frase fecha (past simple). Não disse quando, a conta continua (present perfect: have / has + particípio).

4. As duas formas lado a lado

FormaComo montaExemploEm português
Past simpleverbo no passadoWe opened our second office in 2018.Abrimos o segundo escritório em 2018.
Present perfecthave / has + particípioWe have delivered more than four hundred projects.Já entregamos mais de quatrocentos projetos (e a conta continua).
Present perfect (negativa)have never + particípioWe have never lost a client to a competitor.Nunca perdemos um cliente para um concorrente.
Present perfect (com it)has + particípioDataside has grown every year.A Dataside cresceu todo ano.

5. Palavras que escolhem a forma por você

Com past simple (fecha)Com present perfect (continua)
in 2018, last year, in March, two years ago, yesterdayfor, since, ever, never, already, so far, this year
We hired him last year.
Contratamos ele ano passado.		We have hired forty people so far.
Até agora contratamos quarenta pessoas.

6. For e since: os dois pedem present perfect

PalavraVem antes deExemploEm português
foruma duração (quanto tempo)Dataside has been in the market for fifteen years.A Dataside está no mercado há quinze anos.
sinceum ponto de partida (desde quando)I have been the CEO since 2009.Sou CEO desde 2009.

O português usa o presente (“sou CEO desde 2009”, “estamos aqui há quinze anos”). O inglês não aceita: com for e since é sempre have / has + particípio.

7. Onde o português atrapalha

“Sou CEO desde 2009” traduzido palavra por palavra vira I am CEO since 2009, que está errado. O certo é I have been CEO since 2009.

Data junto com present perfect. “Ano passado abrimos um escritório”: tem data, então é past simple. Last year we opened an office. Nunca last year we have opened.

A empresa continua sendo it. Então é has, não have: Dataside has grown.

8. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Em vez deDigaPor quê
I am CEO since 2009I have been CEO since 2009Com since é present perfect.
Last year we have opened an officeLast year we opened an officeTem data: a frase fecha.
Dataside have grownDataside has grownEmpresa é it: has.
We are in the market since fifteen yearsWe have been in the market for fifteen yearsQuinze anos é duração: for.

9. O texto do Pre-class, trecho a trecho

O mesmo texto do Grammar in Context da Lesson 02, dividido em partes. Leia o inglês primeiro e só depois confira o português.

There is a moment in every first meeting when a buyer stops asking what the company does and starts asking what it has done. The two questions sound similar and they are not. The first one can be answered by anybody with a website. The second one can only be answered by a company with a history, and English keeps a separate shape for it.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Existe um momento em toda primeira reunião em que o comprador para de perguntar o que a empresa faz e começa a perguntar o que ela já fez. As duas perguntas parecem iguais e não são. A primeira qualquer um com um site consegue responder. A segunda só uma empresa com história consegue responder, e o inglês tem uma forma separada para ela.

Dataside has been operating for fifteen years. We have delivered more than four hundred projects. We have never lost a client to a competitor. None of those three sentences carries a date, and that is the whole point.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Dataside has been operating for fifteen years (a Dataside opera há quinze anos). We have delivered more than four hundred projects (já entregamos mais de quatrocentos projetos). We have never lost a client to a competitor (nunca perdemos um cliente para um concorrente). Nenhuma dessas três frases tem data, e é exatamente essa a ideia.

The shape is have or has plus the past participle, and it does one job: it says the count is still running. Four hundred projects today, four hundred and one next month. Compare that with we opened our second office in 2018. The year is named, the sentence closes, and nothing about it can change. That is the past simple, and it is the right shape whenever the time is on the table.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A forma é have ou has mais o particípio, e ela faz uma coisa só: diz que a conta ainda está correndo. Quatrocentos projetos hoje, quatrocentos e um no mês que vem. Compare com we opened our second office in 2018 (abrimos o segundo escritório em 2018). O ano foi dito, a frase fecha, e nada nela pode mudar. Isso é o past simple, e é a forma certa sempre que o tempo está na mesa.

The rule underneath both is short enough to carry into a meeting: name the time and the sentence closes; leave the time out and you are still counting. With for and since the count is explicit (for takes a length of time, since takes a starting point) and both of them require the present perfect, always.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A regra por trás das duas é curta o bastante para levar para uma reunião: disse o tempo, a frase fecha; deixou o tempo de fora, você ainda está contando. Com for e since a conta fica explícita (for vem com uma duração, since com um ponto de partida) e os dois exigem o present perfect, sempre.

Two traps cost a Portuguese speaker the most, and they are both traps of translation rather than of grammar. The first is since with the simple present. In Portuguese the equivalent sentence sits comfortably in the present tense, so the direct translation arrives as I am CEO since 2009. English will not take it: it has to be I have been CEO since 2009.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Duas armadilhas custam mais caro para quem fala português, e as duas são de tradução, não de gramática. A primeira é since com o presente simples. Em português a frase equivalente fica confortável no presente (“sou CEO desde 2009”), então a tradução direta sai I am CEO since 2009. O inglês não aceita: tem que ser I have been CEO since 2009.

The second trap is a named time glued to a present perfect (Last year we have opened an office) and the fix is to drop back to the past simple: Last year we opened an office. And underneath both, the permanent one: a company is an it, so it takes has. Not Dataside have grown. Dataside has grown.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A segunda armadilha é um tempo com nome grudado num present perfect (Last year we have opened an office), e o conserto é voltar para o past simple: Last year we opened an office (ano passado abrimos um escritório). E por baixo das duas, o erro de sempre: empresa é it, então leva has. Não Dataside have grown, e sim Dataside has grown (a Dataside cresceu).

opened: tem ano, a frase fecha.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- The Present Perfect for Company History

GRAMMAR

Name the time and the sentence closes. Leave the time out and you are still counting.

JobFormExample
Started before, still true nowhas / have + participle + for or sinceDataside has operated for fifteen years.
A count that can still go uphas / have + past participleWe have delivered four hundred projects.
A life experience, with no dateever · neverWe have never lost a client.
News, with the result still herejust · already · yetWe have just signed the term sheet.
Finished, and the time is namedpast simple + a closed timeWe opened the office in 2018.
The trapa named time kills the present perfectNot Last year we have grown. Say Last year we grew.
The other trapsince never takes the present simpleNot I am CEO since 2009. Say I have been CEO since 2009.
The permanent targetthe company is an it, so hasNot Dataside have grown. Say Dataside has grown.

Never: I am CEO since 2009 · Last year we have opened an office · Dataside have delivered · We never have lost a client

Lesson 03 -- Pre-class

The Story a Buyer Actually Checks -- Duration, Process and the Data Room

A buyer stops asking what you do and starts asking how long it has been running. Key words: an acquirer, due diligence, valuation, a synergy, a pipeline, proprietary, to leverage, to disrupt. Structure: the present perfect continuous.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

An acquirer -- the company that is buying, as opposed to the one being bought
"The acquirer sent us a list of forty documents before the second call."
Due diligence -- the deep check a buyer runs on everything you have claimed
"Due diligence has been running for six weeks."
Valuation -- the price the two sides agree the company is worth
"Our valuation depends on how concentrated the revenue is."
A synergy -- the value that only exists if the two companies are joined
"They see a synergy between our engineers and their client base."
A pipeline -- the deals or projects you expect to close but have not closed yet
"Our pipeline has been growing every quarter since March."
Proprietary -- built by you, owned by you, and not available anywhere else
"The forecasting engine is proprietary. Nobody else has it."
To leverage -- to use something you already own to get a result somewhere else
"They want to leverage our models across their whole portfolio."
To disrupt -- to change an industry so much that the old way stops working
"AI has been disrupting consulting for three years already."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

An acquirer
Due diligence
Valuation
A synergy
A pipeline
Proprietary

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

There is a question a serious buyer asks that a curious one never does. Not what do you do, and not even what have you done, but how long has it been running. The reason is not politeness. A result can be a lucky quarter; a process that has not stopped for two years is much harder to fake, and much harder to lose. So the shape English uses for duration is the shape that fills a due diligence call: we have been building the engine since 2022, the pipeline has been growing every quarter since March, they have been running diligence for six weeks.

The form is have or has plus been plus the -ing verb, and the test that chooses it is one question: can you answer how many, or only how long? We have signed four contracts answers how many, so it is the ordinary present perfect — a counted result. We have been signing contracts since March answers how long, so it is the continuous — an activity still under way. Both are true about the same three months. They simply point at different things, and a buyer listens for which one you reach for first.

Two things trip a Portuguese speaker here. The first is that Portuguese covers this ground with the simple present tense, so the direct translation arrives as we are doing this since six weeks, which is wrong twice over — wrong tense and wrong preposition. It has to be we have been doing this for six weeks, with for before a length and since before a starting point. The second is that some verbs refuse the -ing entirely because they describe a state rather than an activity: be, have in the sense of owning, know, need, want, mean. Not I have been knowing him for ten years. I have known him for ten years. And underneath all of it, the permanent one: the pipeline, the company and the market are each an it, so they take has, never have.

Explicação em portuguêsPresent perfect continuous: have been + -ingToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. É a forma que diz que uma atividade começou no passado e continua acontecendo agora: “We have been building the engine since 2022” (estamos construindo o motor desde 2022). Em português a gente diz isso com o presente (“estamos construindo desde 2022”, “faz seis semanas que eles fazem a due diligence”).

2. Quando usar. Quando a pergunta é há quanto tempo (how long): processos que não pararam, coisas em andamento numa due diligence. Se a pergunta é quantos (how many), você volta para o present perfect simples da aula 2.

3. A regra em uma frase. have / has + been + verbo com -ing, para atividade que ainda está em andamento.

4. Como monta

SujeitoFormaExemploEm português
I, you, we, theyhave been + -ingWe have been building the forecasting engine since 2022.Estamos construindo o motor de previsão desde 2022.
he, she, ithas been + -ingOur pipeline has been growing every quarter.Nosso pipeline vem crescendo todo trimestre.
theyhave been + -ingThey have been running due diligence for six weeks.Eles estão fazendo a due diligence há seis semanas.
PerguntaHow long has / have ... been + -ing?How long has the engine been in production?Há quanto tempo o motor está em produção?

5. Quantos ou há quanto tempo?

A pergunta é...FormaExemploEm português
how many? (um resultado contado)have + particípioWe have signed four new contracts this quarter.Assinamos quatro contratos novos neste trimestre.
how long? (uma atividade em andamento)have been + -ingWe have been signing contracts since March.Estamos fechando contratos desde março.

As duas frases podem ser verdade sobre os mesmos três meses. Uma mostra o resultado, a outra mostra o processo.

6. Verbos que não aceitam -ing

Alguns verbos descrevem um estado, não uma atividade, e por isso nunca ganham -ing: be, have (no sentido de ter, possuir), know, need, want, mean.

Com eles, use o present perfect simples:
I have known their head of corporate development for ten years. (Conheço o diretor de desenvolvimento corporativo deles há dez anos.)

E não I have been knowing him.

7. Onde o português atrapalha

Presente no lugar do perfect. “Fazemos isso há seis semanas” traduzido direto vira we are doing this since six weeks, errado duas vezes: no tempo verbal e na preposição. O certo é we have been doing this for six weeks.

For x since (igual à aula 2): for + duração (six weeks), since + ponto de partida (March, 2022).

Pipeline, empresa, mercado: tudo it. Então é has been, nunca have been.

8. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- The Present Perfect Continuous

How many is a result. How long is a process. English uses a different shape for each.

Lesson 04 -- Pre-class

If You Move on That, We Move on This -- The Language of Deal Terms

Three things you can do when somebody puts a condition on the table, and only one of them costs nothing. Key words: an earnout, closing, contingent, a threshold, a clause, binding, a non-disclosure agreement, to walk away from. Structure: the first conditional for deal terms.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

An earnout -- part of the price that is only paid if the company hits agreed targets later
"Half the price was an earnout tied to three years of revenue."
Closing -- the day the deal legally completes and the money moves
"If closing slips past June, the whole timetable changes."
Contingent -- depending on something else happening first
"The second payment is contingent on client retention."
A threshold -- the number you have to reach before something is triggered
"If revenue passes the threshold, the earnout pays in full."
A clause -- one specific rule inside a contract, written separately
"There is a clause that protects the engineering team for two years."
Binding -- legally forcing both sides to do what the document says
"The term sheet is not binding, except for the confidentiality section."
A non-disclosure agreement -- the contract that stops either side repeating what it learns
"Nothing goes in the data room before the non-disclosure agreement is signed."
To walk away from -- to end the negotiation and accept that there is no deal
"Knowing what you would walk away from is what gives you room to move."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

An earnout
Closing
Contingent
A threshold
A clause
Binding

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text -- tap Listen to hear each paragraph -- then answer the questions.

There are only three things you can do when somebody puts a condition on the table. You can accept it, you can refuse it, or you can trade. Accepting costs money. Refusing costs information, because the moment you say a flat no the other side stops proposing, and their proposals were the only thing telling you what they actually want. Trading costs nothing, and English has one sentence shape built for it: if you move on the threshold, we will move on the timetable.

The shape is if plus the present simple, then will plus the bare verb. Both halves are about the future, and that is exactly what makes it counterintuitive: the if half stays in the present anyway. If you accept, not if you will accept. This is the single most expensive mistake a Portuguese speaker makes in a negotiation, because Portuguese marks the future in both halves and the direct translation puts will where English will not take it. There is also a quieter version: unless, which simply means if not, and which draws a hard line while sounding like a condition. We will not sign anything unless the clause protects the team is a refusal that nobody in the room will hear as a refusal.

One shape close to it does something different. If revenue passes the threshold, the earnout pays in full keeps both halves in the present, and that is not an offer at all — it is a rule that fires by itself, the way a contract clause does. Use it for what is already agreed, never for what you are still negotiating. And the permanent target does not go away just because there is an if in front of it: after if, he, she and it still take the -s. Not if the buyer accept. If the buyer accepts.

The same three moves happen again on paper, and on paper they have their own vocabulary. A payment that arrives only if something else happens first is contingent on it. A document that legally forces both sides to do what it says is binding, and most of a term sheet is not binding at all, apart from the confidentiality section and the non-disclosure agreement both sides have signed weeks before anything else. Closing is the day the deal legally completes and the money moves, and every condition in the document points at that date. If a payment is contingent on a number, the number decides. If it is contingent on a person, you have handed that person the deal.

And there is one condition you write for yourself, before the first meeting. Decide what you will walk away from, and write it down. If you have not decided that, every condition they propose sounds reasonable, because you have nothing to measure it against. If revenue passes the threshold, the earnout pays in full is a rule you have already accepted; if you move on the threshold, we will move on the timetable is still an offer. The founders who negotiate well are not the ones who talk the most. They are the ones who know, before the room fills up, which line they will not cross.

Explicação em portuguêsIf + presente, will + verbo; unlessToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. É a frase de troca: “se você fizer X, a gente faz Y”. Em inglês: “If you move on the threshold, we will move on the timetable” (se vocês cederem na meta, a gente cede no cronograma). As duas metades falam do futuro, mas a metade do if fica no presente.

2. Quando usar. Em toda negociação, quando você quer trocar em vez de aceitar ou recusar. Também para estabelecer limites de um jeito que não soa como “não”: unless.

3. A regra em uma frase. If + presente, depois will + verbo puro. Nunca will depois de if.

4. As três frases de condição desta aula

FormaPara quêExemploEm português
If + presente, will + verbouma proposta, algo que ainda vai ser decididoIf you move on the threshold, we will move on the timetable.Se vocês cederem na meta, a gente cede no cronograma.
unless = if notum limite que soa como condiçãoWe will not sign anything unless the clause protects the team.Não assinamos nada a menos que a cláusula proteja o time.
If + presente, presenteuma regra já combinada, que acontece sozinhaIf revenue passes the threshold, the earnout pays in full.Se a receita passa da meta, o earnout paga integral.

A terceira não é proposta: é como uma cláusula de contrato. Use para o que já está acordado, nunca para o que ainda está negociando.

5. Por que o “se” fica no presente

Em português a gente usa o futuro do subjuntivo nas duas metades: “se você aceitar, a gente vai fechar”. A tradução direta põe will dos dois lados.

O inglês não aceita will depois de if. A metade do if fica no presente simples:
If you accept, we will close in June. (Se vocês aceitarem, fechamos em junho.)
E não if you will accept.

E o -s da aula 1 continua valendo depois do if: If the buyer accepts our number. (Se o comprador aceitar o nosso número.)

6. Palavras de contrato que andam com essas frases

PalavraO que éExemploEm português
contingent onque só acontece se outra coisa acontecer antesThe second payment is contingent on client retention.O segundo pagamento depende da retenção de clientes.
bindingque obriga legalmenteMost of the term sheet is not binding.A maior parte do term sheet não é vinculante.
closingo dia em que o negócio se completa e o dinheiro muda de mãoIf closing slips past June, the timetable will change.Se o closing passar de junho, o cronograma muda.
walk away fromdesistir do negócio por causa de algoDecide what you will walk away from.Decida do que você vai desistir.

Contingent e depend pedem on, nunca of.

7. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Em vez deDigaPor quê
If you will accept, we will closeIf you accept, we will closeDepois de if, presente.
If the buyer accept our numberIf the buyer accepts our numberComprador é he / she: -s.
We will not sign if not the clause protects the teamWe will not sign unless the clause protects the teamUnless já quer dizer “se não”.
contingent of client retentioncontingent on client retentionÉ sempre on.

Trading costs nothing, and English has one sentence shape built for it: if you move on the threshold, we will move on the timetable.

If you accept, not if you will accept. This is the single most expensive mistake a Portuguese speaker makes in a negotiation, because Portuguese marks the future in both halves and the direct translation puts will where English will not take it.

And the permanent target does not go away just because there is an if in front of it: after if, he, she and it still take the -s. Not if the buyer accept. If the buyer accepts.

EM PORTUGUÊS

If revenue passes the threshold, the earnout pays in full (se a receita passa da meta, o earnout paga integral) deixa as duas metades no presente, e isso não é proposta nenhuma: é uma regra que dispara sozinha, como uma cláusula de contrato. Use para o que já está acordado, nunca para o que você ainda está negociando. E o erro de sempre não some só porque tem um if na frente: depois de if, he, she e it continuam levando o -s. Não if the buyer accept, e sim if the buyer accepts.

The same three moves happen again on paper, and on paper they have their own vocabulary. A payment that arrives only if something else happens first is contingent on it. A document that legally forces both sides to do what it says is binding, and most of a term sheet is not binding at all, apart from the confidentiality section and the non-disclosure agreement both sides have signed weeks before anything else.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Os mesmos três movimentos acontecem de novo no papel, e no papel eles têm vocabulário próprio. Um pagamento que só chega se outra coisa acontecer antes é contingent on (condicionado a) essa coisa. Um documento que obriga legalmente os dois lados a fazer o que está escrito é binding (vinculante), e a maior parte de um term sheet não é vinculante, fora a parte de confidencialidade e o non-disclosure agreement (acordo de confidencialidade) que os dois lados assinaram semanas antes de tudo.

Closing is the day the deal legally completes and the money moves, and every condition in the document points at that date. If a payment is contingent on a number, the number decides. If it is contingent on a person, you have handed that person the deal.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Closing é o dia em que o negócio se completa legalmente e o dinheiro muda de mão, e toda condição do documento aponta para essa data. Se um pagamento depende de um número, o número decide. Se depende de uma pessoa, você entregou o negócio na mão dessa pessoa.

And there is one condition you write for yourself, before the first meeting. Decide what you will walk away from, and write it down. If you have not decided that, every condition they propose sounds reasonable, because you have nothing to measure it against. The founders who negotiate well are not the ones who talk the most. They are the ones who know, before the room fills up, which line they will not cross.

EM PORTUGUÊS
E tem uma condição que você escreve para você mesmo, antes da primeira reunião. Decida do que você vai walk away from (desistir, levantar da mesa), e escreva. Se você não decidiu isso, toda condição que eles propõem parece razoável, porque você não tem com o que comparar. Os fundadores que negociam bem não são os que falam mais. São os que sabem, antes de a sala encher, qual linha eles não vão cruzar.

9. Teste rápido (toque para ver a resposta)

a) If you ___ (move) on the threshold, we will move on the timetable.

move: depois de if, presente.

b) If closing slips past June, the whole timetable ___ (change).

will change: a outra metade leva will.

c) We will not sign anything ___ the clause protects the team.

unless: “a menos que”.

d) If revenue passes the threshold, the earnout ___ (pay) in full.

pays: regra já combinada, as duas metades no presente.

e) If the buyer ___ (accept) our number, we can close in June.

accepts: o comprador é he / she.

B Information, because the other side stops proposing.
C Time, because the negotiation restarts.

A Because Portuguese marks the future in both halves, so the direct translation puts will where English will not take it.

3. When should you keep both halves in the present?

C When it is a rule that is already agreed and fires by itself, not something you are still negotiating.

A The payment becomes binding, so it cannot be renegotiated.
B You have handed that person the deal.
C Closing has to move to a later date.
5. Why does the text say you should decide what you would walk away from before the first meeting?
A Because the buyer will ask you for that list.
B Because the threshold cannot be renegotiated afterwards.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- The First Conditional for Deal Terms

GRAMMAR

The condition stays in the present. Only the result gets a future.

The trapwill never follows ifNot if you will accept. Say if you accept.

Lesson 05 -- Pre-class

The Room Where Three People Ask at Once -- Certainty, Possibility and Obligation

A committee call with three voices and three accents. Key words: integration, a transition, retention, governance, compliance, a deliverable, a roadmap, to hand over. Structure: modal verbs for certainty, possibility and obligation.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Integration -- the work of joining two companies into one after the deal closes
"Integration is where most acquisitions actually fail."
A transition -- the period when control moves from one side to the other
"We can deliver a transition in ninety days."
Retention -- keeping the people you need after they find out the company was sold
"Retention is the number the committee will ask about first."
Governance -- who is allowed to decide what, and who has to be told
"Governance has to be agreed before closing, not after."
Compliance -- following the rules and being able to prove that you did
"All our contracts must meet European compliance standards."
A deliverable -- a specific thing you have promised to hand over by a date
"Every deliverable in the plan has a name and a date on it."
A roadmap -- the plan of what happens when, over the next months or years
"The roadmap should survive the transition without being rewritten."
To hand over -- to pass responsibility for something to another person or team
"I will hand over the client relationships myself, one at a time."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Integration
A transition
Retention
Governance
Compliance
A deliverable

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Two sentences about the same ninety days. We will deliver the transition in ninety days. We can deliver the transition in ninety days. One word apart, and they are not variations of each other — they are different sizes of promise. The first is a commitment somebody can hold you to, and in a committee meeting it goes into the minutes as one. The second says you are capable, which is a statement about your company rather than a promise about the future. Founders reach for the first when they mean the second, usually because it sounds more confident, and six months later somebody reads it back to them.

English has a small set of these words — will, can, could, may, might, must, should — and each one sets a level. Could, may and might are possibilities that cost you nothing and buy you room: three of the eleven might take a call from a competitor admits a risk without promising an outcome, and it makes the rest of what you say more credible rather than less. Should is almost certain, based on evidence. Must is a rule. And there is one mechanical relief in all of this: after any of these words the verb is bare. No -s, no to, no ending at all. She can deliver, never she can delivers.

Two habits travel here from Portuguese and both are audible. The first is stacking two of them together, because the idea arrives as a single word in Portuguese and needs two in English: not we will can deliver, but we will be able to deliver. The second is must pointed at another person. In American business English you must send me the analysis sounds like an order from a superior, which is almost never what the speaker meant. For obligation that comes from outside, use have to; for a request, use could you; and keep must for rules and compliance, where it belongs.

Explicação em portuguêsModal verbs: will, can, could, may, might, should, mustToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. São palavrinhas que vão antes do verbo e dizem o quanto você tem certeza ou o quanto aquilo é obrigatório. Em português a gente faz isso com “vou”, “posso”, “pode ser que”, “deveria”, “tenho que”. Em inglês cada nível tem uma palavra própria.

2. Quando usar. Numa reunião com comitê, onde tudo o que você diz vira ata. “We will deliver” é promessa e alguém vai cobrar. “We can deliver” é capacidade. Escolher a palavra certa é escolher o tamanho do compromisso.

3. A regra em uma frase. Depois de qualquer modal, o verbo vai puro: sem -s, sem to, sem terminação nenhuma.

4. Cada palavra, um nível

PalavraO que dizExemploEm português
willpromessa, compromissoWe will deliver the transition in ninety days.Vamos entregar a transição em noventa dias. (vão cobrar)
cancapacidadeWe can deliver the transition in ninety days.Conseguimos entregar a transição em noventa dias.
shouldquase certo, com base em evidênciaThe numbers should be ready by Friday.Os números devem ficar prontos até sexta.
could / may / mightpossibilidadeThree of the eleven might take a call from a competitor.Três dos onze podem atender uma ligação de um concorrente.
mustregra, obrigação formalEvery contract must meet European compliance standards.Todo contrato tem que cumprir as normas europeias de compliance.
have to / has toobrigação que vem de foraGovernance has to be agreed before closing.A governança tem que ser acordada antes do closing.

Admitir uma possibilidade com might não enfraquece você: deixa o resto do que você diz mais crível.

5. O verbo depois do modal fica puro

She can deliver. (e não she can delivers)

She can hand over the client relationships herself. (Ela mesma pode passar os relacionamentos com os clientes.)

It must meet the standards. (e não it must to meet)

Atenção: have to não é modal de verdade, então ele mesmo leva o -s: Governance has to be agreed.

6. Onde o português atrapalha

Dois modais juntos. “Vamos poder entregar” tem duas ideias, e em inglês não dá para colar will + can. Use will be able to: By June we will be able to deliver it. (Em junho vamos conseguir entregar.)

Must apontado para outra pessoa. “Você tem que me mandar a análise” em português é normal. You must send me the analysis, no inglês americano de negócios, soa como ordem de chefe. Para pedir, use could you: Could you send me the analysis? Para obrigação que vem de fora, have to. Guarde must para regra e compliance.

Lesson 06 -- Pre-class

What Would Dataside Look Like in Five Years? -- The Language of the Long View

A founder answered the five-year question three times, on three pages, and only then understood what she had been asked. Key words: a moat, headcount, to reinvest, runway, to spin off, a trade-off, to double down, dilution. Structure: the second conditional for hypothetical futures.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A moat -- an advantage a competitor cannot copy quickly, even with money
"Our moat is not the client list. It is the twelve engineers who built the platform."
Headcount -- the total number of people a company employs
"Headcount has doubled in three years, and margin has not moved."
To reinvest -- to put profit back into the business instead of taking it out
"For eleven years we reinvested everything, and nobody took a dividend."
Runway -- how many months a company can keep operating on the cash it already has
"Eighteen months of runway sounds comfortable until you try to raise in month sixteen."
To spin off -- to separate one part of a company into a new independent business
"If we spun off the analytics unit, it would need its own board."
A trade-off -- something you give up in order to get something else
"Every one of the three futures had the same trade-off: speed or control."
To double down -- to commit even more to a choice you have already made
"We doubled down on the vertical we already owned and refused every other market."
Dilution -- the fall in your share of ownership when new shares are issued
"The dilution would take me from seventy-one percent to something near forty."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

A moat
Headcount
To reinvest
Runway
To spin off
A trade-off
To double down
Dilution

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

An investor asks what your company would look like in five years. Nobody believes the forecast, including the person who wrote it, so the question is not really about the fifth year. It is a test of whether you have ever seriously imagined a company other than the one you already decided to build. Answering it needs a sentence shape that describes something untrue: if we opened an office in New York, we would need a different kind of leader.

The shape is if plus the past simple, then would plus the bare verb. Nothing in that sentence is about the past. The past form is not marking time here — it is marking distance: this has not happened, and it may never happen. That is the whole difference from the shape you already know. If we open in New York, we will need a leader there is a plan somebody is going to decide. If we opened in New York, we would need a leader there is a picture nobody has agreed to yet. Same office, completely different meeting.

Two details finish the structure. With the verb be, this shape takes were for every person, including I and it: if I were you, if the market were stronger. And when the result is a maybe rather than a certainty, could or might replaces would: if we spun it off, we might lose the platform team.

Two traps, both expensive. The first: would never follows if. Portuguese carries this idea with a dedicated verb form in the first half and a conditional in the second, and the direct translation puts would in both halves — a mistake that marks a speaker as translating rather than thinking. Say if we opened, not if we would open. The second is the permanent target turned inside out: after would, the verb takes no ending at all. Not he would needs. He would need.

Explicação em portuguêsIf + passado, would + verboToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. É a frase de hipótese: “se a gente abrisse em Nova York, precisaríamos de outro tipo de líder”. Em inglês: “If we opened an office in New York, we would need a different kind of leader.” O verbo vai para o passado, mas a frase não fala do passado: o passado aqui marca distância, quer dizer “isso não aconteceu e pode nunca acontecer”.

2. Quando usar. Quando um investidor pergunta como a Dataside seria daqui a cinco anos, ou quando você quer explorar um cenário sem se comprometer com ele. Se é um plano de verdade, que você vai decidir, use a forma da aula 4 (if + presente, will).

3. A regra em uma frase. If + passado, depois would + verbo puro.

4. Plano ou hipótese?

FormaO que dizExemploEm português
If + presente, will (aula 4)um plano que alguém vai decidirIf we open in New York, we will need a leader there.Se a gente abrir em Nova York, vamos precisar de um líder lá.
If + passado, would (aula 6)uma imagem que ninguém aprovou aindaIf we opened in New York, we would need a leader there.Se a gente abrisse em Nova York, precisaríamos de um líder lá.

Mesmo escritório, reunião completamente diferente.

5. Os detalhes da estrutura

CasoComo ficaExemploEm português
Verbo bewere para todo mundo, até I e itIf I were you, I would wait.Se eu fosse você, eu esperaria.
Verbo be com itwereIf the market were stronger, we would raise now.Se o mercado estivesse mais forte, captaríamos agora.
Resultado só possívelcould / might no lugar de wouldIf we spun it off, we might lose the platform team.Se a gente separasse essa área, poderíamos perder o time de plataforma.
Número no resultadowould + verbo puroIf we spun off the analytics unit, headcount would fall by forty.Se separássemos a unidade de analytics, o quadro cairia em quarenta pessoas.

6. Onde o português atrapalha

Would dos dois lados. Em português são duas formas diferentes (“se a gente abrisse, precisaríamos”), e a tradução direta acaba pondo would nas duas metades. O would nunca vem depois do if: if we opened, e não if we would open.

Depois de would, verbo puro. É o -s ao contrário: aqui o verbo não leva nada. He would need, e não he would needs.

7. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Em vez deDigaPor quê
If we would open in New YorkIf we opened in New YorkDepois de if, passado; nunca would.
If I was youIf I were youNa hipótese, were para todos.
He would needs a different leaderHe would need a different leaderDepois de would, verbo puro.

8. O texto do Pre-class, trecho a trecho

O mesmo texto do Grammar in Context da Lesson 06, dividido em partes. Leia o inglês primeiro e só depois confira o português.

An investor asks what your company would look like in five years. Nobody believes the forecast, including the person who wrote it, so the question is not really about the fifth year. It is a test of whether you have ever seriously imagined a company other than the one you already decided to build.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Um investidor pergunta como a sua empresa seria daqui a cinco anos. Ninguém acredita na previsão, nem quem escreveu, então a pergunta não é de verdade sobre o quinto ano. É um teste para ver se você já imaginou a sério uma empresa diferente daquela que você já decidiu construir.

Answering it needs a sentence shape that describes something untrue: if we opened an office in New York, we would need a different kind of leader.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Para responder, você precisa de uma forma de frase que descreve algo que não é verdade: if we opened an office in New York, we would need a different kind of leader (se a gente abrisse um escritório em Nova York, precisaríamos de outro tipo de líder).

The shape is if plus the past simple, then would plus the bare verb. Nothing in that sentence is about the past. The past form is not marking time here: it is marking distance. This has not happened, and it may never happen. That is the whole difference from the shape you already know.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A forma é if mais o past simple, depois would mais o verbo puro. Nada nessa frase fala do passado. A forma do passado aqui não marca tempo: marca distância. Isso não aconteceu, e pode nunca acontecer. Essa é toda a diferença para a forma que você já conhece.

If we open in New York, we will need a leader there is a plan somebody is going to decide. If we opened in New York, we would need a leader there is a picture nobody has agreed to yet. Same office, completely different meeting.

EM PORTUGUÊS
If we open in New York, we will need a leader there (se a gente abrir em Nova York, vamos precisar de um líder lá) é um plano que alguém vai decidir. If we opened in New York, we would need a leader there (se a gente abrisse em Nova York, precisaríamos de um líder lá) é uma imagem com a qual ninguém concordou ainda. Mesmo escritório, reunião completamente diferente.

Two details finish the structure. With the verb be, this shape takes were for every person, including I and it: if I were you, if the market were stronger. And when the result is a maybe rather than a certainty, could or might replaces would: if we spun it off, we might lose the platform team.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Dois detalhes completam a estrutura. Com o verbo be, essa forma usa were para todas as pessoas, inclusive I e it: if I were you (se eu fosse você), if the market were stronger (se o mercado estivesse mais forte). E quando o resultado é um talvez e não uma certeza, could ou might entra no lugar de would: if we spun it off, we might lose the platform team (se a gente separasse essa área, poderíamos perder o time de plataforma).

Two traps, both expensive. The first: would never follows if. Portuguese carries this idea with a dedicated verb form in the first half and a conditional in the second, and the direct translation puts would in both halves, a mistake that marks a speaker as translating rather than thinking. Say if we opened, not if we would open. The second is the permanent target turned inside out: after would, the verb takes no ending at all. Not he would needs. He would need.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Duas armadilhas, as duas caras. A primeira: would nunca vem depois de if. O português carrega essa ideia com uma forma própria na primeira metade (“abrisse”) e um condicional na segunda (“precisaríamos”), e a tradução direta põe would nas duas metades, um erro que mostra que a pessoa está traduzindo em vez de pensar. Diga if we opened, e não if we would open. A segunda é o erro de sempre ao contrário: depois de would, o verbo não leva terminação nenhuma. Não he would needs, e sim he would need.

opened: depois de if, passado.

b) If I ___ you, I would wait for the second offer.

c) If we spun off the analytics unit, headcount ___ (fall) by forty.

would fall.

d) If we spun it off, we ___ lose the platform team. (talvez)

might (ou could).

3. Why does the text call if we would open an expensive mistake?

The past form is not time. It is distance from the truth.

Lesson 07 -- Pre-class

From Founder to Seller -- The Language of What Changed

A buyer is not buying what you still do. He is buying what you stopped doing, and when. Key words: to bootstrap, a hire, to step back, a successor, burnout, to delegate, a blind spot, to outgrow. Structure: used to and would for past habits and states.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

To bootstrap -- to build a company using only its own revenue, with no outside money
"We bootstrapped the whole thing, so there was never anybody else to do the work."
A hire -- a person you bring into the company, seen as a decision
"The commercial director was the hire I did not want to make."
To step back -- to stop being involved in running something day to day
"Who runs this company on the Monday after you step back?"
A successor -- the person who takes your job when you leave it
"There is no single successor. Three people each own a piece of it."
Burnout -- the exhaustion that comes from working too hard for too long
"I was two months from burnout and I did not know the word yet."
To delegate -- to give a task or a decision to somebody else to handle
"I did not use to delegate anything on the technical side."
A blind spot -- a weakness in your own judgement that you cannot see yourself
"I have the same blind spot. I still read every proposal."
To outgrow -- to become too big for something that used to fit
"The company outgrew the way I used to run it, and that is the good news."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

To bootstrap
A hire
To step back
A successor
Burnout
To delegate
A blind spot
To outgrow

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

A buyer looking at a founder-led company asks one question that decides everything else: does this business still need the person who built it? He will not ask it in those words. He will ask what you used to do, and he will listen for what you no longer do. The list of things you handed over is the only evidence he accepts, and it needs a form: I used to sign every contract myself, and I stopped in 2019.

There are two forms for a life you have left behind, and they are not interchangeable. Used to plus the bare verb covers everything: a habit you had and stopped, and also a situation that is simply no longer true. I used to write every proposal. The company used to be six people in one room. Would plus the bare verb covers only the first of those two. It works for an action you repeated, usually with a time marker attached: every Friday I would sit with the engineers until the build passed. It does not work for a state. The company would be six people is not English.

One event, on one date, takes neither. It takes the plain past simple: in 2019 we hired our first commercial director. And the negative and the question drop the final letter, which is the detail almost everybody gets wrong in writing: I did not use to delegate, not did not used to.

The expensive confusion is with a completely different structure that looks almost identical. I am used to working alone means it feels normal to me now. I used to work alone means it does not happen any more. One is about the present and takes the -ing form; the other is about the past and takes the bare verb. Saying the wrong one in a diligence meeting tells the buyer the opposite of what you meant. And the permanent target does not disappear either: after used to and after would, the verb carries no ending at all. Not he used to signs. He used to sign.

Explicação em portuguêsUsed to e would para o que mudou; e a diferença para be used toToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. São as formas de falar de um hábito ou de uma situação que era assim e não é mais. Em português a gente usa o imperfeito: “eu assinava todo contrato”, “a empresa era seis pessoas”. Em inglês: “I used to sign every contract”, “The company used to be six people.”

2. Quando usar. Quando o comprador quer saber se a empresa ainda depende de você. Ele vai perguntar o que você fazia antes e vai prestar atenção no que você não faz mais. A lista do que você passou adiante é a prova que ele aceita.

3. A regra em uma frase. used to + verbo puro serve para hábito e para situação que acabou. would + verbo puro serve só para ação repetida. Fato com data é past simple.

4. Três formas para o passado

FormaServe paraExemploEm português

The company used to be six people in one room.		Eu assinava todo contrato pessoalmente.

would + verbosó ação repetida (normalmente com marcador de tempo)Every Friday I would sit with the engineers until the build passed.Toda sexta eu sentava com os engenheiros até o build passar.
past simpleum fato, uma dataIn 2019 we hired our first commercial director.Em 2019 contratamos nosso primeiro diretor comercial.

Would não serve para situação: the company would be six people não é inglês. Na dúvida, used to sempre funciona.

5. Negativa e pergunta: o -d cai

Quando entra o did, o used perde o -d (o passado já está no did):

I did not use to delegate anything on the technical side. (Eu não delegava nada da parte técnica.)

Did you use to run the sales team? (Você comandava o time de vendas?)

É o detalhe que quase todo mundo erra por escrito: did not used to está errado.

Trocar uma pela outra numa due diligence diz ao comprador o contrário do que você queria.

O imperfeito não tem uma tradução só. “Eu assinava” pode ser I used to sign ou I would sign; “a empresa era pequena” só pode ser used to be (ou was).

Verbo puro depois de used to e de would. Não he used to signs. He used to sign.

Used to works for everything you left behind. Would only works for things you did.

Lesson 08 -- Pre-class

What the Data Shows -- The Language of the Board Pack

Forty pages became eleven, and almost every sentence lost its subject. Key words: a benchmark, churn, a margin, to forecast, an outlier, to audit, a baseline, recurring revenue. Structure: the passive voice for executive reporting.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A benchmark -- the outside number other companies are measured against
"Every number in the pack is shown against a market benchmark."
Churn -- the share of clients who leave in a period
"Churn is measured on client count, not on revenue."
A margin -- what is left of the revenue once the costs are taken out
"Headcount doubled in three years and the margin did not move."
To forecast -- to say what the numbers will be before they happen
"The forecast was missed by nine percent."
An outlier -- a number so far from the others that it distorts the picture
"One quarter was an outlier and the whole company built a story on it."
To audit -- to check the numbers formally, from outside the company
"The accounts were audited by Vieira and Marsh in March."
A baseline -- the starting number you measure every change against
"We set a baseline of twelve trailing months and showed every number against it."
Recurring revenue -- money that arrives every month without being sold again
"One page of recurring revenue was the page the buyer read twice."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

A benchmark
Churn
A margin
To forecast
An outlier
To audit
A baseline
Recurring revenue

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

There are two ways to report the same fact to a board. My team missed the forecast puts a person in the sentence, and the room immediately starts deciding whether somebody should be blamed. The forecast was missed by nine percent takes the person out, and the room starts deciding what to do next. The facts are identical. The conversation is not, and in a negotiation the difference between those two conversations is worth money.

The form is two verbs, always: a form of be, then the past participle. The forecast was missed. Churn is measured on client count. The accounts were audited in March. The first verb does all the work you can hear: it carries the tense and it agrees with the subject. The second one never changes. This is the piece a Portuguese speaker most often loses, because the same idea is carried in that language by a single short word attached to the verb, and the direct translation produces a sentence with only one verb in it. The forecast missed by nine percent is not English.

When the actor matters after all, it comes back on the end with by: the accounts were audited by Vieira and Marsh. Use it when the name changes what the sentence is worth — an auditor's name does, and a colleague's name usually does not. And when nothing is being done to the subject, none of this applies: two deals moved into the next quarter stays as it is, because nobody moved them.

One warning that has nothing to do with grammar and everything to do with the room. This form can be used to hide, and every experienced listener knows it. A mistake was made tells a board that somebody is not saying who, and you have spent your credibility to save one word. So the rule that goes with the form is short: take the person out when the person is not the point, and never when the person is you.

Explicação em portuguêsVoz passiva: be + particípioToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. É o jeito de contar um fato sem dizer quem fez. Em vez de “My team missed the forecast” (meu time errou a previsão), você diz “The forecast was missed by nine percent” (a previsão ficou nove por cento abaixo). Em português a gente faz isso com “foi” + particípio (“as contas foram auditadas”) ou com o “se” (“mede-se o churn por cliente”).

2. Quando usar. Em relatório para o conselho e em negociação, quando o que importa é o fato e não quem fez. Com a pessoa na frase, a sala começa a procurar culpado. Sem a pessoa, a sala começa a decidir o que fazer.

3. A regra em uma frase. Dois verbos, sempre: uma forma de be (que muda com o tempo e com o sujeito) e depois o particípio (que nunca muda).

4. Como monta

TempoForma de beExemploEm português
Presente, uma coisais + particípioChurn is measured on client count.O churn é medido pelo número de clientes.
Passado, uma coisawas + particípioThe forecast was missed by nine percent.A previsão ficou nove por cento abaixo.
Passado, várias coisaswere + particípioThe accounts were audited in March.As contas foram auditadas em março.
Presente, várias coisasare + particípioEvery figure is shown against a trailing twelve-month baseline.Cada número é mostrado contra a média dos últimos doze meses.

O primeiro verbo faz todo o trabalho que dá para ouvir: carrega o tempo e concorda com o sujeito. O particípio fica sempre igual.

5. Quando a pessoa importa: by

Se o nome muda o valor da frase, ele volta no final com by:

The accounts were audited by Vieira and Marsh. (As contas foram auditadas pela Vieira and Marsh.)

O nome de um auditor muda o valor da frase. O nome de um colega, normalmente não.

6. Quando NÃO é passiva

Se ninguém fez nada com o sujeito, a frase fica como está:

Two deals moved into the next quarter. (Dois negócios passaram para o próximo trimestre.) Ninguém moveu os negócios; eles simplesmente andaram.

7. Onde o português atrapalha

O verbo que some. Em português dá para dizer a mesma coisa com uma palavrinha colada no verbo (“perdeu-se a previsão”, “mede-se o churn”), e a tradução direta sai com um verbo só: the forecast missed by nine percent. Isso não é inglês. Faltou o was.

A passiva também serve para esconder, e todo mundo sabe. A mistake was made diz ao conselho que alguém não está dizendo quem. Regra: tire a pessoa quando a pessoa não é o assunto, e nunca quando a pessoa é você.

GRAMMAR

Two verbs, always. The first one carries the tense; the second one never changes.

Lesson 09 -- Pre-class

What They Said at the Table -- The Language of the Debrief

Whoever writes the recap owns the deal, because what everybody remembers three weeks later comes out of that email and not out of the room. Key words: a rebuttal, to reiterate, a caveat, to paraphrase, a recap, to push back, to escalate, a takeaway. Structure: reported speech with backshifting.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A rebuttal -- an answer that argues back against an objection, point by point
"If it is a position and not a mistake, you will need a rebuttal by Friday."
To reiterate -- to say the same thing again on purpose, so that it holds
"Should I reiterate the June date in the same email?"
A caveat -- a condition or warning attached to what somebody has just agreed
"I said we could hold the price, with one caveat about the timing."
To paraphrase -- to say what somebody said, in your own words, without changing it
"I will paraphrase it in the recap and copy him, so nothing is invented later."
A recap -- a short written summary of what was said and decided
"The recap goes out with three lines and one takeaway."
To push back -- to disagree with something openly, and say why
"Their finance lead pushed back on the retention number."
To escalate -- to move a question up to somebody senior enough to answer it
"Then we escalate that one, in writing, today."
A takeaway -- the one thing somebody will actually do after the meeting
"The takeaway is theirs to confirm, not yours to announce."

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

In a negotiation, what was agreed is not what was said in the room. It is what was written afterwards. Somebody leaves the meeting, sends an email, and three weeks later everybody argues from that email and nobody remembers the call. So the person who can repeat other people accurately, in English, controls the record — and the person who cannot has handed that job to the other side.

The mechanism is one step backwards. Everything the person said moves one tense further into the past. We are ready becomes he said they were ready. The pool was agreed becomes she said the pool had been agreed, because it was already past when she spoke. The modals move with it: can becomes could, will becomes would, must becomes had to. The pronouns move too, and so does the time: tomorrow becomes the next day.

A reported question stops being a question. It loses the auxiliary, it loses the question order and it loses the question mark: can you hold the price? becomes he asked whether we could hold the price. Keeping the original order — he asked what did we want — is the single most common mistake in this structure, and it is audible immediately. The other one is smaller and just as visible in writing: tell needs a person after it and say does not. He told me. He said that. Never he said me.

There is one exception worth knowing, because it belongs to your world. When the thing reported is still true at the moment you are speaking, the step back becomes optional: he said the threshold is fourteen percent is correct if it still is. And the permanent target survives here too: in the present, the reporting verb keeps its ending. She says, not she say. Finally, one rule that is not grammar at all. Report the sentence, not your feeling about the sentence. If the buyer said the margin was too thin, say he said the margin was too thin. You are allowed to disagree in the next sentence; you are not allowed to edit his on the way home.

Explicação em portuguêsReported speechToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. É a forma de contar o que outra pessoa falou, sem as aspas. Em português a gente faz isso o tempo todo: “Ele disse que eles estavam prontos.”

2. Quando usar. No recap depois da call, no e-mail para o comprador (“você disse que…”), ou quando você conta para o seu sócio ou para o conselho o que o outro lado falou na reunião.

3. A regra em uma frase. Quando o verbo que abre a frase está no passado (said, told, asked), tudo o que a pessoa disse anda um passo para trás no tempo. O português faz parecido, só que o inglês é bem mais rígido com isso.

4. Como o verbo muda

O que ele falouComo você contaEm português
“We are ready to move in June.”He said they were ready to move in June.presente → passado
Ele disse que eles estavam prontos.
“We are reviewing the numbers.”She said they were reviewing the numbers.-ing no presente → -ing no passado
Ela disse que estavam revisando os números.
“The pool was agreed.”She said the pool had been agreed.passado → had + particípio
Ela disse que o pool já tinha sido acordado.
“We can hold the price.”He said they could hold the price.can → could
Ele disse que podiam segurar o preço.
“We will fund the pool.”He said they would fund the pool.will → would
Ele disse que iam financiar o pool.
“You must sign by Friday.”She said we had to sign by Friday.must → had to
Ela disse que a gente tinha que assinar até sexta.

5. O que mais muda junto

Quem fala muda: we vira they, our vira their, you vira we (se era com você). Igual ao português.

O tempo muda: today → that day · tomorrow → the next day · next week → the following week · yesterday → the day before.

6. Pergunta contada deixa de ser pergunta

Some o do/does/did, a ordem volta a ser de frase normal (sujeito + verbo) e some o ponto de interrogação.

Pergunta de sim ou não: use whether (ou if).
“Can you hold the price?” → He asked whether we could hold the price.
Ele perguntou se a gente conseguia segurar o preço.

Pergunta com what, when, how much: mantém a palavra e segue com ordem normal.
“What do you want?” → He asked what we wanted.
Ele perguntou o que a gente queria.

7. Say ou tell?

Tell pede a pessoa logo depois: He told me the price was final.
Say não leva a pessoa: He said the price was final.
Os dois significam “ele disse”. A diferença é só se a pessoa aparece ou não.

8. A exceção que vale para você

Se o que a pessoa disse continua verdade agora, você pode manter o presente: He said the threshold is fourteen percent. Está certo, desde que o número ainda seja 14%.

9. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Em vez deDigaPor quê
He said me the price was final.He told me the price was final.Com a pessoa, é tell.
He asked what did we want.He asked what we wanted.Pergunta contada não usa did.
He said they will hold the price.He said they would hold the price.Will anda um passo para trás.
She say the numbers are audited.She says the numbers are audited.No presente, she continua pedindo o -s (Lesson 1).

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Reported Speech with Backshifting

GRAMMAR

Everything moves one step further into the past. Report the sentence, not your feeling about it.

JobFormExample
Reporting a statementevery verb steps one back"We are ready" → He said they were ready.
Already past when they spokepast → had + participle"It was agreed" → She said it had been agreed.
The modals move toocan→could · will→would · must→had to"We can hold" → He said they could hold.
Reporting a questionasked whether / asked what + normal order"Can you hold?" → He asked whether we could hold.
Naming who you spoke totell takes a person, say does notHe told me. Not he said me.
Still true right nowthe step back becomes optionalHe said the threshold is fourteen percent.
The trapa reported question is not a questionNot he asked what did we want. Say he asked what we wanted.
The permanent targetthe reporting verb keeps its endingShe says the numbers are audited. Not she say.

Never: he said me · he asked what did we want · he said they will hold · she say

Lesson 10 -- Pre-class

Precision at the Table -- The Language of Which One, Exactly

Two versions of the same paragraph: one is the brochure and one is the business, and the difference is a half-sentence attached to every claim. Key words: a referral, a vertical, tenure, a backlog, to bundle, an incumbent, a footprint, to onboard. Structure: relative pronouns in defining and non-defining clauses.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A referral -- a new client who arrived because an existing one recommended you
"Our largest client, which arrived through a referral in 2019, has renewed four times."
A vertical -- one industry segment that a company sells into
"The two verticals where we have the deepest experience are banking and logistics."
Tenure -- how long somebody has been with the company
"The eleven engineers whose tenure is over five years built the platform."
A backlog -- work that has already been sold and has not been delivered yet
"How much of the backlog is under signed contract, and how much is verbal?"
To bundle -- to sell several separate things together as one offer
"He bundled three products into one offer and described it with the wrong commas."
An incumbent -- the supplier who already holds the contract you are trying to win
"They built the platform that the incumbent supplier could not replace."
A footprint -- the set of places and markets where a company actually operates
"The two countries where we have people, and the six where we only have clients."
To onboard -- to bring a new client or employee through the first weeks of the process
"The process that a new client goes through in the first ninety days."
