Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Two sentences can contain the same facts and be worth very different amounts. We serve large clients across many verticals is true and unusable. The two verticals where we have the deepest experience are banking and logistics is the same claim with a half-sentence attached, and that half-sentence is the whole difference: it turns a description into something a buyer can go and verify. In a room where somebody is deciding what your company is worth, a claim nobody can check is a claim nobody pays for.

The half-sentence starts with a small word that points back at the noun in front of it. Who for people, which or that for things, where for places and situations, whose for what belongs to somebody. The partner who ran the call. The platform that the incumbent could not replace. The verticals where we are strongest. The engineers whose tenure is over five years. When the pronoun is the object of its own clause, you can drop it entirely: the client we onboarded in March is complete English.

Then there is the punctuation, and it is not decoration. Without commas, the clause is telling the reader which one: the client that arrived through a referral has renewed four times means there are several clients and this is the one being talked about. With commas, the thing was already unique and the clause only adds a detail: our largest client, which arrived through a referral, has renewed four times means there is exactly one largest client. And in that second kind, that is not allowed — after a comma it is always which or who.

Two traps. The first is small and audible: the subject is not repeated after the pronoun. Portuguese allows the speaker to pick the subject up again inside the clause, and the direct translation produces the engineers who they built the platform. The pronoun already is the subject. The second trap is the permanent target in a new place: the verb inside the clause agrees with the noun in front of it, not with the pronoun. The client who has renewed. The clients who have renewed.

Explicação em portuguêsRelative clauses: who, which, that, where, whoseToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. É um pedaço de frase que vem logo depois de um substantivo para dizer qual é, ou para dar um detalhe sobre ele. Em português é o nosso “que”, “onde” e “cujo”: “o cliente que renovou”, “as verticais onde somos mais fortes”.

2. Quando usar. Sempre que uma frase sua soar vaga para o comprador. “We serve large clients” ninguém consegue checar. “The two clients who renewed four times are in banking” dá para conferir, e o que dá para conferir vale dinheiro.

3. A regra em uma frase. Depois do substantivo vem uma palavrinha que aponta para ele (who, which, that, where, whose) e, em seguida, o resto da informação.

4. Qual palavrinha usar

PalavraPara quêExemploEm português
who (ou that)pessoasThe partner who ran the call has done eleven deals.O sócio que conduziu a call já fez onze negócios.
which ou thatcoisasThe platform that the incumbent could not replace.A plataforma que o fornecedor atual não conseguiu substituir.
wherelugares e situaçõesThe two verticals where we have the deepest experience.As duas verticais onde temos mais experiência.
whosede quem é (posse)The engineers whose tenure is over five years.Os engenheiros cujo tempo de casa passa de cinco anos.

Em português falado quase ninguém usa “cujo”. Em inglês whose é normal, até em conversa.

5. Quando dá para tirar o that

Olhe o que vem logo depois da palavrinha:

Se vem outro sujeito (we, they, the buyer), pode tirar.
The client (that) we onboarded in March. → The client we onboarded in March.
O cliente que a gente integrou em março.

Se vem o verbo direto, não pode tirar.
The partner who ran the call. (sem o who a frase quebra)

6. A vírgula muda o sentido

Como ficaO que quer dizerExemplo
Sem vírgulaDiz qual: existem vários, e eu estou falando deste.The client that arrived through a referral has renewed four times.

Depois de vírgula, nunca use that: é sempre which (coisa) ou who (pessoa).

7. Onde o português atrapalha

Não repita o sujeito. Em português falado a gente às vezes retoma (“os engenheiros que eles construíram…”). Em inglês o who já é o sujeito.
The engineers who built the platform. (e não who they built)

O verbo concorda com o substantivo que vem antes.
The client who has renewed. (o cliente que renovou)
The clients who have renewed. (os clientes que renovaram)

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Relative Pronouns, Defining and Non-Defining

GRAMMAR

No commas means which one. Commas mean by the way.

JobFormExample
Saying which personwho (or that)The partner who ran the call has done eleven deals.
Saying which thingwhich or thatThe platform that the incumbent could not replace.
Saying which place or situationwhereThe two verticals where we have the deepest experience.
Saying whose it iswhose + nounThe engineers whose tenure is over five years.
Adding a detail about something uniquetwo commas, and never thatOur largest client, which arrived through a referral, has renewed.
Dropping the pronounpossible when it is the object of the clauseThe client (that) we onboarded in March.
The trapthe subject is not repeated after the pronounNot the engineers who they built it. Say the engineers who built it.
The permanent targetthe verb agrees with the noun in frontThe client who has renewed. The clients who have renewed.

Never: the partner which · the engineers who they built it · our largest client, that arrived · the clients who has renewed

Lesson 11 -- Pre-class

Saying What You Mean -- The Verbs That Decide the Next Verb

One small word can turn a decision into a doubt: stop to think and stop thinking are not the same promise. Key words: a priority, to postpone, to intend, to refuse, to insist on, upfront, bluntly, a commitment. Structure: verbs followed by the infinitive or by the -ing form.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A priority -- the thing that you decide to do first, before everything else
“Our priority is to close the deal before December.”
To postpone -- to move an event or a decision to a later date
“We postponed signing until the audit was finished.”
To intend -- to have a clear plan to do something
“The buyer intends to keep the brand for at least two years.”
To refuse -- to say clearly that you will not do something
“We refused to sign the exclusivity clause in its current form.”
To insist on -- to say firmly that something must happen
“They insisted on keeping me as CEO until the end of the transition.”
Upfront -- paid or agreed at the beginning, before the rest
“We want sixty percent of the price upfront, at closing.”
Bluntly -- in a very direct way, without making it softer
“To put it bluntly, we will not accept less than that number.”
A commitment -- a promise that people expect you to keep
“Staying for two years is a commitment, not a hope.”

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

A priority
To postpone
To intend
To refuse
To insist on
Upfront
Bluntly
A commitment

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

A buyer asked a founder whether he would stay after the sale. He answered, I stopped to think about it. He meant the opposite: he had stopped thinking about it, because he had already decided. The buyer wrote down that the founder was still unsure, and the next three weeks of negotiation started from that note. One small word changed what he meant.

In English, the first verb decides the form of the verb that follows it. Some verbs take the infinitive with to: we intend to keep the brand, they refused to sign, we agreed to postpone the closing. These are verbs that look forward, toward something that has not happened yet. Other verbs take the -ing form: we avoid promising dates, they suggested waiting, we postponed signing. And after a preposition, it is always -ing: they insisted on keeping me, I look forward to meeting you. In that last one, to is a preposition, not part of the verb, and that is why the verb after it takes -ing.

Then there are the verbs that change meaning. Stop doing something means you no longer do it; stop to do something means you pause in order to do it. Remember to send the contract is a job for later; I remember sending the contract is a memory. Try to cut costs means make an effort; try cutting costs means test the idea and see what happens.

The trap for a Portuguese speaker is the sentence that sounds natural in your head: I suggest to wait, I look forward to meet you, they want that we sign. None of them is English. Say I suggest waiting, I look forward to meeting you, they want us to sign. A buyer will understand all three, but the correct version is the one that sounds like a person who has done this before.

Explicação em portuguêsVerbo + to ou verbo + -ingToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. Em inglês, o primeiro verbo decide a forma do verbo que vem depois. Alguns pedem to + verbo (I intend to stay), outros pedem o verbo com -ing (I avoid promising). Em português quase sempre usamos o infinitivo nos dois casos (“pretendo ficar”, “evito prometer”), e é por isso que confunde.

2. Quando usar. Em toda negociação. Na hora de dizer o que você concorda em fazer, o que recusa, o que adiou e o que parou de fazer. Em alguns verbos (stop, remember, try) a forma muda o sentido, e o comprador anota o sentido errado.

3. A regra em uma frase. Verbo que olha para a frente (plano, decisão, promessa) pede to; atividade, e tudo que vem depois de preposição, pede -ing.

4. Os dois grupos

GrupoVerbosExemploEm português
+ towant, plan, intend, agree, refuse, decide, expect, promiseWe intend to keep the brand.Pretendemos manter a marca.
+ -ingavoid, suggest, consider, postpone, keep, finishWe postponed signing the contract.Adiamos a assinatura do contrato.
preposição + -inginsist on, look forward to, thank you for, interested inThey insisted on keeping me.Eles insistiram em me manter.
pessoa + towant, ask, expect, need + alguémThey want us to sign.Eles querem que a gente assine.

“Sugiro esperar” vira I suggest waiting, e não I suggest to wait.

“Fico no aguardo de te conhecer” vira I look forward to meeting you. Aqui o to é preposição, então vem -ing.

Cuidado com o try. “I will try to stay” soa como “vou tentar ficar”, ou seja, dúvida. Se é promessa, diga I intend to stay.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Verb + to or Verb + -ing

GRAMMAR

Verbs that look forward take to. Activities, and anything after a preposition, take -ing.

JobFormExample
A plan or a decisionverb + to + verb (want, plan, intend, agree, refuse, decide, expect)We intend to keep the brand for two years.
An activityverb + -ing (avoid, suggest, consider, postpone, keep, finish)We postponed signing until the audit was finished.
After a prepositionpreposition + -ingThey insisted on keeping me for two years.
Asking someone else to actverb + person + to + verbThey want us to sign before December.
Stopstop doing = no longer do it · stop to do = pause in order to do itI stopped checking every invoice. I stopped to check one invoice.
Rememberremember to do = a job for later · remember doing = a memoryRemember to send the contract. I remember sending it.
Trytry to do = make an effort · try doing = test itTry to cut costs. Try cutting the meeting to twenty minutes.
The trapto as a preposition takes -ingI look forward to meeting you. Not to meet.

Never: I suggest to wait · they want that we sign · I look forward to meet you · we avoid to promise

The Language of Performance -- Reviewing What People Do, Not Who They Are

A buyer reads your team through the way you describe it: activities are evidence, adjectives are not. Key words: a performance review, accountable, to underperform, ownership, to mentor, a KPI, to exceed expectations, candid. Structure: the -ing form as a subject and after prepositions, it is worth + -ing, adjective + to.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A performance review -- a meeting where a manager and an employee talk about how well the employee has worked
“Her performance review is on Friday, and it will be the first one after the audit.”
Accountable -- responsible for a result and expected to explain it
“Marina is accountable for every project that we deliver to banks.”
To underperform -- to do less well than people expected
“Telling someone they are underperforming is hard, but waiting is worse.”
Ownership -- the attitude of treating a problem as your own job to solve
“Taking ownership of the late project was the moment I knew he was ready.”
To mentor -- to help a less experienced person grow by giving advice over a long time
“Mentoring the two new managers will be her main goal next year.”
A KPI -- a number that shows how well a person or a team is doing
“The KPI that matters most for delivery is projects finished on time.”
To exceed expectations -- to do better than what was planned or expected
“She exceeded expectations on every KPI except hiring.”
Candid -- honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable
“I want a candid review, not a polite one.”

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Most founders are good at hiring and bad at reviewing. Hiring feels like building something; reviewing feels like judging somebody you hired yourself. So the review gets postponed, and when it finally happens it is full of adjectives: she is great, he is a bit slow. A buyer who reads those reviews learns nothing about the team, and the team is a large part of what the buyer is paying for.

Performance language in English depends on one form: the -ing form used as a noun. Managing the largest account is her real job. Missing two deadlines in a row is the problem, not the person. Hiring slowly was the best decision we made in 2020. The subject of each sentence is an activity, and that is exactly the point: you are reviewing what somebody does, not who they are.

The same form follows every preposition: she is good at keeping clients, thank you for staying late, instead of blaming the team. Two more patterns complete the toolkit. It is worth plus -ing says something deserves the effort: it is worth investing in her. An adjective plus to says how hard or easy something is, or how you felt: she is hard to replace, I was surprised to see the numbers.

The trap for a Portuguese speaker is the first word of the sentence. In Portuguese the bare verb can open a sentence, and the direct translation produces hire slowly was the best decision, which is not English. Put -ing on the verb and the sentence works: hiring slowly was the best decision. The same thing happens after worth: not it is worth to invest, but it is worth investing.

2. Quando usar. Em avaliação de desempenho, feedback e quando o comprador pergunta sobre o seu time. Frase que começa por uma atividade fala do que a pessoa faz, não de quem ela é, e isso é o que o comprador consegue avaliar.

3. A regra em uma frase. Atividade como sujeito e verbo depois de preposição levam -ing; it is worth leva -ing; adjetivo + to + verbo diz se é fácil, difícil ou como você se sentiu.

Lesson 13 -- Pre-class

Handling the Hard Questions -- The Short Verbs That Keep You in Control

Under pressure, a phrasal verb is shorter than an explanation, and it says that something was already done. Key words: to bring up, to back up, to rule out, to look into, to follow up, to figure out, to hold off, to walk someone through. Structure: business phrasal verbs and where the object goes.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

To bring up -- to start talking about a subject in a conversation
“Thank you for bringing it up. It is a fair question.”
To back up -- to support a claim with evidence
“We can back it up with the audit report from March.”
To rule out -- to decide that something is not possible
“We have ruled out a second office this year.”
To look into -- to investigate or check something carefully
“We looked into it last month and found the cause.”
To follow up -- to contact someone again to continue a conversation
“I will follow up with your lawyer on Friday.”
To figure out -- to find the answer to a problem by thinking about it
“We figured out why the margin fell in the third quarter.”
To hold off -- to wait before you do something
“We are holding off on hiring until the deal closes.”
To walk someone through -- to explain something to a person step by step
“Let me walk you through the numbers.”

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

To bring up
To back up
To rule out
To look into
To follow up
To figure out
To hold off

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Every due diligence has one meeting where the questions get harder. A buyer brings up the client you lost last year, or a number that does not match. Founders who handle this well do not have better answers; they have better verbs. They say we looked into it, we can back it up, we have ruled that out. Short verbs, and every one of them says that something was already done.

These are phrasal verbs: a verb plus a small word, with a meaning you cannot always guess from the parts. Bring up a subject is to start talking about it. Back up a claim is to give the evidence. Rule out an option is to decide it is not possible. Look into a problem is to investigate it. Follow up is to come back to it later, figure out is to find the answer, hold off is to wait before acting, and walk somebody through something is to explain it step by step.

The grammar is in where the object goes. With most of them, a noun can go before or after the small word: back up the claim or back the claim up. A pronoun can only go in the middle: back it up, rule it out, bring it up. A few never separate: you look into it, never look it into. Walk through takes the person in the middle: let me walk you through the numbers. And when hold off is followed by an activity, Lesson 11 comes back: we are holding off on signing.

Under pressure, the temptation is to answer with a long explanation. A phrasal verb is shorter, and it sounds like the person in control. The buyer asks about the lost client; you say we looked into it, here is what we figured out, and I can walk you through it. Three verbs, and the meeting moves on.

Explicação em portuguêsPhrasal verbs de negócios e onde fica o objetoToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. Phrasal verb é um verbo + uma palavrinha (up, out, into, through, off) que, juntos, ganham um sentido próprio. Look é olhar, mas look into é investigar. Em português isso vira um verbo só (“investigar”, “comprovar”, “descartar”).

2. Quando usar. Quando o comprador faz a pergunta difícil. Um phrasal verb é curto, soa natural e diz que algo já foi feito: “we looked into it” (investigamos), “we can back it up” (temos como comprovar).

3. A regra em uma frase. Substantivo pode ir antes ou depois da palavrinha; pronome (it, them) vai sempre no meio: back it up. A exceção é look into, que nunca se separa: look into it.

Em português o pronome vai antes ou depois do verbo inteiro (“comprovar isso”), então sai back up it. Em inglês: back it up.

Lesson 14 -- Pre-class

Reading the Room -- The Signals That Tell You What Comes Next

On a fast call, you do not need every word. You need the signal before the important part. Key words: a ballpark figure, bandwidth, traction, optics, a guardrail, a carve-out, a non-starter, to circle back. Structure: signpost phrases in spoken English (having said that, to put it differently, here’s the thing).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A ballpark figure -- a number that is close but not exact
“Can you give us a ballpark figure for the synergies?”
Bandwidth -- the time and energy a team has for more work
“We don’t have the bandwidth for a second project this quarter.”
Traction -- progress or support that is growing
“The deal is gaining traction with their board.”
Optics -- how a decision looks to other people
“The optics of a price cut right now are bad.”
A guardrail -- a limit that keeps a process safe
“We need guardrails on the integration timeline.”
A carve-out -- a part of a company that is kept out of a deal
“The training unit could be a carve-out.”
A non-starter -- an idea that has no chance of being accepted
“A minority stake is a non-starter for us.”
To circle back -- to return to a subject later in a conversation
“Let’s circle back to the price on Friday.”

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

On a call with American investors, a founder rarely loses the meeting because of grammar. He loses it in the first ten seconds of a fast answer, when he is still translating the last sentence. The good news is that native speakers help you more than you think: before an important idea, they almost always send a signal.

These signals are called signposts. Having said that means the next idea goes in the opposite direction. To put it differently means the same idea is coming again, in simpler words, so it is your second chance. Here’s the thing means the important part is next. Let me be clear introduces a firm position, often a non-starter. And let’s table that closes a subject for now, but somebody will circle back to it later.

Speed is the other problem. In fast speech, going to sounds like gonna, want to sounds like wanna, and kind of sounds like kinda. You do not need to say them, but you need to hear them. When a buyer says we’re gonna need a ballpark figure, she is asking for a number, and she is asking for it soon.

The strategy is simple. Do not try to catch every word. Listen for the signpost, and predict what kind of sentence comes next. If you miss something, check it: If I understood correctly, you are saying that… Nobody in the room will think less of you. They will think you are listening.

Explicação em portuguêsSignposts: os sinais que avisam o que vem depoisToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. Signpost é uma expressão curta que o falante usa ANTES de uma ideia importante, como uma placa na estrada. Ela não traz a informação, ela avisa que tipo de informação vem: um problema, uma repetição, o ponto principal.

2. Quando usar. Quando você está ouvindo um nativo rápido e não consegue pegar tudo. Se você reconhece o sinal, já sabe o que esperar da frase seguinte, mesmo perdendo algumas palavras. E dois deles são para você falar: If I understood correctly… e Could you clarify…?

3. A regra em uma frase. Não tente entender todas as palavras: ouça o sinal e preveja a próxima frase. Se perdeu, confira em voz alta em vez de ficar calado.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Signposts in Spoken English

GRAMMAR

The signpost comes first. It tells you what kind of sentence comes next.

SignpostWhat comes nextExample
Having said thatthe opposite directionThe deal has traction. Having said that, the price is still open.
To put it differentlythe same idea, simplerTo put it differently, we need a smaller carve-out.
Here’s the thingthe most important pointHere’s the thing: we don’t have the bandwidth.
Let me be cleara firm positionLet me be clear: a minority stake is a non-starter.
Let’s table thatthe subject stops for nowLet’s table that and circle back on Friday.
If I understood correctlya check (you say it)If I understood correctly, you need a ballpark figure.
Could you clarify…?a question (you say it)Could you clarify what you meant by optics?

In fast speech: gonna = going to · wanna = want to · kinda = kind of. Hear them; you do not need to say them.

Lesson 15 -- Pre-class

Presenting Dataside’s Future -- The Five-Part Pitch

Investors buy the future. A pitch that spends four minutes on the past and thirty seconds on the plan sounds like a goodbye. Key words: a value proposition, a growth driver, a target market, to outline, to position, going forward, to expand into, a long-term goal. Structure: will, be going to and the present continuous for the future.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A value proposition -- the main reason a client should buy from you
“Our value proposition is simple: your data, ready for AI in ninety days.”
A growth driver -- something that makes a company grow
“Banking is our biggest growth driver this year.”
A target market -- the group of clients a company wants to sell to
“Our target market is mid-sized banks in Latin America.”
To outline -- to describe the main points of something
“Let me outline the plan in three steps.”
To position -- to make people see a company in a particular way
“We want to position Dataside as the data partner for AI.”
Going forward -- from now on, in the future
“Going forward, we will report every quarter in English.”
To expand into -- to start doing business in a new market
“We are going to expand into Mexico next year.”
A long-term goal -- something you want to achieve in many years
“Our long-term goal is to work with the top fifty banks in the region.”

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

A growth driver
A target market
To outline
To position

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

Many founders pitch like historians. They spend four minutes on the past (fifteen years, three hundred people, the first client) and thirty seconds on the future. But an investor is not buying the past. She is buying what the company is going to become, and she wants to hear it in a clear structure.

A good pitch has five parts: who we are, what we have done, where we are going, why this deal, and your questions. The first two parts use tenses you already know: Dataside is a data company, we have grown every year since 2015. The third part is where the future lives, and English has three ways to talk about it.

Use be going to for a plan you have already decided: we are going to expand into Mexico next year. Use the present continuous for something already arranged, with a date or a contract: we are opening an office in Austin in March. Use will for a prediction or a promise: this market will double, I will stay as CEO for three years.

The difference matters to a buyer. We are opening an office sounds signed. We are going to open an office sounds decided. We will open an office sounds like a promise, so be ready to back it up. Choose the form that says exactly how sure you are.

Explicação em portuguêsTrês jeitos de falar do futuro: will, be going to e present continuousToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. O inglês não tem um tempo verbal “futuro” só. Tem três formas, e cada uma diz um grau de certeza: going to (decidido), present continuous (combinado, com data) e will (previsão ou promessa).

2. Quando usar. Na parte 3 do pitch, “para onde vamos”. O comprador ouve a forma e entende o quanto aquilo é certo: we are opening soa assinado, we are going to open soa decidido, we will open soa promessa.

3. A regra em uma frase. Plano decidido = going to; já combinado com data = present continuous; previsão, promessa ou decisão na hora = will. Depois de will e de going to, verbo na forma base.

4. As três formas

FormaEm portuguêsExemplo
be going to + verbovamos (plano decidido)We are going to expand into Mexico. (Vamos entrar no México.)
present continuous + datavamos (já combinado)We are opening an office in March. (Vamos abrir um escritório em março, já está fechado.)
will (previsão)vaiThis market will double. (Esse mercado vai dobrar.)
will (promessa)vou, prometoI will stay as CEO for three years. (Vou ficar como CEO por três anos.)
’ll (decisão na hora)vou (decidi agora)I’ll send it today. (Te mando hoje.)

5. Negativa e pergunta

CasoComo ficaExemplo
Negativa com willwon’t + verboWe won’t raise prices.
Negativa com going toam/is/are not going toWe aren’t going to hire this year.
Pergunta com willWill + sujeito + verboWill you stay as CEO?
Pergunta com going toAre you going to + verboAre you going to keep the team?
Terceira pessoasem -s depois de willThe market will grow (nunca will grows).

6. Onde o português atrapalha

Em português usamos “vai” para tudo: “vamos abrir”, “vai crescer”, “vou mandar”. Por isso sai will para tudo, e o comprador ouve promessa onde você só queria dizer plano.

Também sai we will to expand ou we going to expand. Depois de will não tem to; e going to precisa do are: we are going to expand.

7. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

We going to open an office.We are going to open an office.Going to precisa do verbo be.
We will open an office in March. (já assinado)We are opening an office in March.Combinado com data = present continuous.
The market will grows.The market will grow.Depois de will, verbo na forma base.

GRAMMAR

Three forms, three levels of certainty. Choose the one that says how sure you are.

UseFormExample
A plan you have decidedbe going to + verbWe are going to expand into Mexico next year.
Something already arrangedpresent continuous + timeWe are opening an office in Austin in March.
A predictionwill + verbThis market will double in five years.
A promise or offerwill + verbI will stay as CEO for three years.
A decision made nowwill (often ’ll)Good question. I’ll send you the numbers today.
Negativewon’t · am not going toWe won’t raise prices. We aren’t going to hire this year.
QuestionWill…? · Are you going to…?Are you going to keep the team? Will you stay?

Remember: after will, the base verb (it will grow, never it will grows). After going to, the base verb too (we are going to expand).

Lesson 16 -- Pre-class

The Numbers Tell a Story -- Saying Data Like an Investor

“We grew a lot” says nothing. “A thirty percent increase in revenue” says a number someone can check. Key words: a trajectory, EBITDA, a run rate, an addressable market, capital allocation, year-over-year, to break even, to plateau. Structure: noun phrases for data (an increase in, a decline in) and nominalization.
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

A trajectory -- the direction in which something develops over time
“Our growth trajectory has been stable for five years.”
EBITDA -- profit before interest, taxes and some accounting costs
“Our EBITDA margin improved to eighteen percent last year.”
A run rate -- what a company will earn in a year if the current month continues
“Our run rate is now ninety million reais a year.”
An addressable market -- all the possible sales in a market for a product
“Our addressable market in Latin America is still largely untapped.”
Capital allocation -- the decision about where a company invests its money
“Capital allocation went mostly to our AI team.”
Year-over-year -- compared with the same period in the previous year
“We saw a twenty percent year-over-year increase in revenue.”
To break even -- to earn exactly as much as you spend
“The new unit broke even in its second year.”
To plateau -- to stop growing and stay at the same level
“Revenue plateaued in 2023, and then it grew again.”

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

In a data room, every founder has the same numbers on the screen. What changes is how he says them. A weak sentence sounds like this: we grew a lot, and costs went down. A strong sentence sounds like this: a thirty percent year-over-year increase in revenue, and a reduction in operating costs. The second one gives the investor a number she can check.

The tool is the noun phrase. Instead of a verb (grow, fall, reduce), you use a noun (growth, a decline, a reduction) and add the details around it. The pattern is a / an + number + noun + in + what: an increase in EBITDA, a decline in margins, a twelve percent rise in the run rate. Notice the preposition: it is almost always in, not of.

This change from verb to noun is called nominalization, and it makes the number the subject of the sentence. We reduced costs, so we broke even becomes the reduction in costs allowed us to break even. We grew fast becomes our growth trajectory has been stable for five years. The sentence sounds less like a story about you and more like evidence.

Use it for the important numbers, not for every sentence. A good data slide has three or four noun phrases and one clear conclusion: revenue plateaued in 2023, but the increase in the run rate since then shows that the trajectory is back. The numbers do the talking; your job is to give them a clear shape.

Explicação em portuguêsNoun phrases e nominalização: dizer o número como o investidor escreveToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. Noun phrase é um grupo de palavras organizado em volta de um substantivo: a thirty percent increase in revenue (um aumento de trinta por cento na receita). Nominalização é trocar o verbo (reduce) pelo substantivo (reduction), para o número virar o sujeito.

2. Quando usar. Quando você fala de dados com investidor, analista ou conselho. “We grew a lot” não se confere; “a twenty percent year-over-year increase” se confere. Também no slide e no e-mail.

3. A regra em uma frase. a / an + número + substantivo + in + o quê: a twenty percent increase in revenue. A preposição é in, não of.

4. As peças do padrão

a decline inuma queda em/dea decline in margins (uma queda nas margens)
a reduction inuma redução em/dea reduction in costs (uma redução nos custos)
year-over-yearem relação ao ano anteriora twenty percent year-over-year increase (alta de 20% sobre o ano anterior)
to plateauestabilizar, parar de crescerRevenue plateaued in 2023. (A receita estabilizou em 2023.)
to break evenempatar (zero a zero)The unit broke even. (A unidade empatou.)

5. Do verbo para o substantivo

Sales went down a little.There was a small decline in sales.go down → a decline
We sell more every year.We have seen a year-over-year increase in sales.a comparação entra na frase

6. Onde o português atrapalha

Em português dizemos “um aumento de receita”, e sai an increase of revenue. Em inglês a mudança acontece dentro de algo: an increase in revenue. O of só entra antes do número: an increase of twenty percent.

Também tendemos a contar a história com nós como sujeito (“nós crescemos, nós cortamos”). Na nominalização o sujeito é o número, e isso soa como prova, não como opinião.

Lesson 17 -- Pre-class

Hedging at the Highest Level -- Precise When You Are Not Sure Yet

In a negotiation, a number said too firmly becomes a promise, and a number said too softly sounds weak. Hedging gives the number its limits. Key words: indicative, preliminary, subject to, provisional, roughly, in the range of, to leave room for, tentative. Structure: hedging and stance markers (based on, the data suggests, it would appear that).
0%
▼

Stage 1.1: Vocabulary Cards

Vocabulary

Listen to each word and read the example. Tap Listen to hear it.

Indicative -- giving an idea of something, but not final
“This is an indicative price, not a final offer.”
Preliminary -- coming before the final version
“These are preliminary numbers from the first audit.”
Subject to -- depending on something that must happen first
“The offer is subject to due diligence.”
Provisional -- true for now, but it may change later
“We have a provisional date for the signing in May.”
Roughly -- not exactly; about
“Roughly sixty percent of our revenue comes from banks.”
In the range of -- between two numbers, approximately
“We expect a valuation in the range of ninety to one hundred million.”
To leave room for -- to keep space for something to change later
“Let’s leave room for further negotiation on the earnout.”
Tentative -- not certain or fully agreed yet
“We have a tentative agreement on the price.”

Stage 1.2: Matching

Practice

Choose the meaning of each word.

Indicative
Preliminary
Subject to
Provisional
Roughly
In the range of
To leave room for
Tentative

Stage 1.3: Grammar in Context

GRAMMAR

Read the text, then answer the questions.

In a negotiation, the way you say a number matters as much as the number. Say it too firmly, our revenue will be one hundred million next year, and it becomes a promise the buyer will remember. Say it too softly, maybe, I don’t know, perhaps one hundred, and you sound like you do not know your own company.

The solution is hedging: giving a number its limits, on purpose. The strongest hedges point to a source: based on our current pipeline, according to the independent valuation, the data suggests that… Others give a range instead of a point: roughly sixty percent, in the range of ninety to one hundred million, a ballpark figure.

A third group shows that something is not final yet: an indicative price, preliminary numbers, a provisional date, a tentative agreement, an offer subject to due diligence. And a fourth group creates distance between you and the claim: it would appear that the buyer wants more time; there is reason to believe that the market will grow.

Hedging is not weakness. A CEO who says based on our current pipeline, we expect revenue in the range of ninety to one hundred million, subject to two contracts we are still negotiating sounds more precise, not less. He gives the number, the source and the risk, and he leaves room for negotiation without promising too much.

Explicação em portuguêsHedging: dar limites ao número sem parecer fracoToque para abrir: o que é, quando usar, exemplos e o texto acima em português.▼

1. O que é. Hedging é dizer uma afirmação com os limites dela, de propósito: a fonte (based on), a faixa (in the range of), a condição (subject to) ou o grau de certeza (preliminary, tentative).

2. Quando usar. Quando o comprador pergunta um número que ainda não é certo: receita do ano que vem, data de assinatura, preço. Sem hedge, o número vira promessa; com maybe e I don’t know, você soa fraco. O hedge preciso fica no meio.

3. A regra em uma frase. Número + fonte (based on…) ou faixa (in the range of…) + condição (subject to…). Troque maybe e I think por um desses.

4. As expressões da aula

ExpressãoEm portuguêsExemplo
based oncom base emBased on our pipeline, we expect growth. (Com base no nosso pipeline, esperamos crescimento.)
the data suggests thatos dados sugerem queThe data suggests that churn is falling. (Os dados sugerem que o churn está caindo.)
roughly / in the range ofcerca de / na faixa deIn the range of ninety to one hundred million. (Na faixa de 90 a 100 milhões.)
indicative / preliminaryindicativo / preliminarAn indicative price. Preliminary numbers. (Preço indicativo. Números preliminares.)
provisional / tentativeprovisório / ainda não fechadoA provisional date. A tentative agreement. (Data provisória. Acordo preliminar.)
subject tosujeito a, dependendo deSubject to due diligence. (Sujeito à due diligence.)
leave room fordeixar espaço paraLet’s leave room for negotiation. (Vamos deixar espaço para negociar.)

5. Firme demais, suave demais, preciso

Firme demaisSuave demaisPreciso (com hedge)
Revenue will be 100 million.Maybe 100, I don’t know.Based on our pipeline, in the range of 90 to 100 million.
We sign in May.I think May, perhaps.We have a provisional date in May.
The price is 95 million.The price is more or less 95.This is an indicative price, subject to due diligence.

6. Onde o português atrapalha

Em português o “acho que” e o “talvez” resolvem tudo, e saem I think e maybe em toda frase. Para o comprador americano isso soa inseguro. Troque pela fonte: based on our numbers.

Também sai subject of ou subjected to (de “sujeito a”). A expressão é subject to + substantivo, e nada mais.

The offer is subject of due diligence.The offer is subject to due diligence.A preposição é to.

In a negotiation, the way you say a number matters as much as the number. Say it too firmly, our revenue will be one hundred million next year, and it becomes a promise the buyer will remember. Say it too softly, maybe, I don’t know, perhaps one hundred, and you sound like you do not know your own company.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Numa negociação, o jeito de dizer um número importa tanto quanto o número. Diga com firmeza demais, nossa receita será de cem milhões no ano que vem, e isso vira uma promessa que o comprador vai lembrar. Diga suave demais, talvez, não sei, quem sabe cem, e você parece não conhecer a própria empresa.

The solution is hedging: giving a number its limits, on purpose. The strongest hedges point to a source: based on our current pipeline, according to the independent valuation, the data suggests that… Others give a range instead of a point: roughly sixty percent, in the range of ninety to one hundred million, a ballpark figure.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A solução é o hedging: dar limites ao número, de propósito. Os hedges mais fortes apontam para uma fonte: based on our current pipeline (com base no nosso pipeline atual), according to the independent valuation (segundo a avaliação independente), the data suggests that (os dados sugerem que)… Outros dão uma faixa em vez de um ponto: roughly sixty percent (cerca de sessenta por cento), in the range of ninety to one hundred million (na faixa de noventa a cem milhões), um número aproximado.

A third group shows that something is not final yet: an indicative price, preliminary numbers, a provisional date, a tentative agreement, an offer subject to due diligence. And a fourth group creates distance between you and the claim: it would appear that the buyer wants more time; there is reason to believe that the market will grow.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Um terceiro grupo mostra que algo ainda não é final: um preço indicative (indicativo), números preliminary (preliminares), uma data provisional (provisória), um acordo tentative (preliminar, ainda não fechado), uma oferta subject to due diligence (sujeita à due diligence). E um quarto grupo cria distância entre você e a afirmação: it would appear that the buyer wants more time (tudo indica que o comprador quer mais tempo); there is reason to believe that the market will grow (há motivos para acreditar que o mercado vai crescer).

Hedging is not weakness. A CEO who says based on our current pipeline, we expect revenue in the range of ninety to one hundred million, subject to two contracts we are still negotiating sounds more precise, not less. He gives the number, the source and the risk, and he leaves room for negotiation without promising too much.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Hedging não é fraqueza. O CEO que diz com base no nosso pipeline atual, esperamos receita na faixa de noventa a cem milhões, dependendo de dois contratos que ainda estamos negociando soa mais preciso, não menos. Ele dá o número, a fonte e o risco, e deixa espaço para negociar sem prometer demais.

Stage 1.4: Grammar Tip -- Hedging and Stance Markers

GRAMMAR

Give the number, then give it its limits: a source, a range, or a condition.

JobFormExample
Point to a sourcebased on / according to + nounBased on our pipeline, we expect growth.
Point to evidencethe data suggests that + clauseThe data suggests that churn is falling.
Give a rangeroughly / in the range ofIn the range of ninety to one hundred million.
Say it is not finalindicative · preliminary · provisional · tentativeThis is an indicative price.
Add a conditionsubject to + nounThe offer is subject to due diligence.
Create distanceit would appear that + clauseIt would appear that they need more time.
Keep spaceleave room for + nounLet’s leave room for negotiation.

Remember: after the data suggests, the valuation indicates and it would appear, the verb is in the third person: suggests, indicates.

Lesson 1 — Who Is Caio, in English?

Video
Kevin Hale — “How to Pitch Your Startup” (Y Combinator)

Thirty-two minutes on the only thing this lesson asked you to do: say what your company is, in one sentence, to somebody who has never heard of it. He tears apart real founder introductions and rebuilds them. The English is fast, American and unscripted — which is the point.

Tip: write down his one-sentence test, then run the Dataside sentence you built today through it. If it fails, rewrite it before the next lesson.

Watch on YouTube ↗
Talk
Celeste Headlee — “10 ways to have a better conversation” (TED)

Eleven minutes on the habit you said costs you meetings: going quiet instead of saying you did not follow. She is direct about what to do instead, and every one of her ten moves is a sentence you can copy.

Tip: turn English subtitles on the first time and off the second. Write down the two moves you already do, and the one you never do.

Watch on TED ↗
Podcast
In Good Company — Arvind Krishna, CEO of IBM

A CEO of a data and AI company answering the same questions you answered today — what the company does, how it makes money, what he is looking for — at full native speed, with no simplification for a non-native listener.

Tip: the first twelve minutes are enough. Listen once with no notes, then write the three sentences he uses to describe IBM. Compare them with yours.

Listen on YouTube ↗

Lesson 2 — Fifteen Years in Four Paragraphs

Talk
Simon Sinek — “How great leaders inspire action” (TED)

Eighteen minutes on exactly what this lesson was about: the order in which you say things about your company. His argument is that most founders open with what they do and never reach why it matters — which is the mistake Ana Beltran took nine years to fix.

Tip: write down the three-word structure he draws on the board, then rewrite your Dataside opening sentence in that order. Say both versions out loud and choose one.

Watch on TED ↗
Video
Graham Weaver — “How to Win Without Crushing Your Soul” (Stanford GSB)

A private equity founder telling his own fifteen-year story to a room of students. He uses the present perfect the way this lesson taught it, constantly and without thinking about it, and the English is unscripted at native speed.

Tip: count how many times he says I have plus a verb in the first ten minutes. Every one of those is a count he is telling you is still running.

Watch on YouTube ↗
Podcast
In Good Company — Andrea Orcel, CEO of UniCredit

A European bank CEO answering the same two questions you practised today: what the company has already done, and what it has not done yet. He is careful with dates in a way that is worth copying.

Tip: the first fifteen minutes are enough. Write down the two sentences where he names a year, and the two where he deliberately does not.

Listen on YouTube ↗

Lesson 3 — The Story a Buyer Actually Checks

Video
The Finance Storyteller — “Mergers and acquisitions explained”

Twelve minutes of the exact vocabulary you learned today, used the way a buyer uses it: acquirer, valuation, synergy, due diligence. Clear, slow enough to follow, and it puts the eight words into one process from start to finish.

Tip: pause every time one of today's eight words appears and say the Dataside version of that sentence out loud before you press play again.

Watch on YouTube ↗
Talk
Aswath Damodaran — “Valuation in Four Lessons” (Talks at Google)

The most respected valuation teacher in the world explaining, in fast unscripted American English, how a buyer decides what a company is worth. This is the argument that will be used about Dataside whether or not you are in the room.

Tip: an hour is too long for one sitting. Watch fifteen minutes, then write the one sentence you would use to defend the Dataside valuation against what he just said.

Watch on YouTube ↗
Podcast
In Good Company — Marc Rowan, CEO of Apollo

The head of one of the largest private equity firms in the world on how his team looks at a company before buying it. He is describing the person on the other side of your table, in his own words and at his own speed.

Tip: the first twenty minutes are enough. Write down every time he uses has been plus a verb -- each one is a process he is telling you has not stopped.

Lesson 4 — If You Move on That, We Move on This

Talk
William Ury — “The walk from no to yes” (TED)

The co-author of the most used negotiation book in the world on the move this lesson is built around: what to do instead of saying no. Eighteen minutes, and the third idea in it is exactly the sentence you practised today.

Tip: watch once with subtitles and once without. Write down the moment he describes the third side, and say out loud what the third side would be in a Dataside negotiation.

Watch on TED ↗
Video
Oxford Online English — “How to Negotiate in English”

A focused lesson on the exact phrases used to make conditional offers, push back and close in a business negotiation. Slower than the other recommendations, and the closest thing here to a rehearsal.

Tip: pause at every phrase and rebuild it with a real Dataside condition before you continue. Say it out loud -- reading it silently does nothing for this.

Watch on YouTube ↗
Podcast
In Good Company — Howard Marks, co-founder of Oaktree

One of the most careful thinkers in finance on how he decides what a deal is worth and when he walks away. His English is unhurried and precise, which makes it the easiest of these three to follow at full speed.

Tip: the first fifteen minutes are enough. Listen for every conditional he builds -- he almost never states a position without attaching a condition to it.

The single most useful hour on the exact problem of this lesson: speaking well when you are put on the spot and have not prepared the sentence. Matt Abrahams is talking to MBA students, at full native speed, about the committee room you were just in.

Adam Galinsky — “How to speak up for yourself” (TED)

Fifteen minutes on the range between sounding too soft and sounding too strong -- which is exactly what choosing between might, can and will does to you in a room full of people you do not control.

Lesson 7 — From Founder to Seller

Podcast
How I Built This — “KAYAK: Paul English”

A founder who built a company, ran it for years and sold it, telling the whole story in the first person. This is the grammar of today for an hour without a break, and the interviewer keeps asking exactly the question you practised: what did you used to do back then?

Tip: write down every sentence you hear that starts with I used to or contains would for a past habit. Aim for ten. You will get there before minute thirty.

Ben Horowitz — “Delegation for a Startup CEO”

Short and blunt, from somebody who ran a company of six hundred people before he started investing. He describes the exact moment a founder has to stop doing the thing he is best at, which is the hardest sentence in this lesson to say out loud about yourself.

Tip: after watching, say his argument back in your own words, out loud, using I used to three times. Do not write it first.

Talk
WorkLife with Adam Grant — “Burnout Is Everyone's Problem”

The organizational psychologist on why exhaustion is a design problem and not a personal failure. Clear, unhurried American English, and one of the eight words from this lesson is the subject of the whole episode.

Tip: listen once for the argument and once for the stories. In the second pass, note how often he describes a past habit rather than a single event — that choice is the grammar of this lesson.

Lesson 9 — What They Said at the Table

Video
Chris Voss — “The Mirroring Technique”

The former lead hostage negotiator at the FBI on the cheapest move in any negotiation: repeating the other person's own words back to them. It is the spoken version of what this lesson practises in writing, and he shows why it makes people keep talking.

Tip: try it on your next call in Portuguese first, then in English. Repeat the last three words the other person said and then stay silent, and count how long they keep going.

Watch on YouTube ↗
Podcast
Hidden Brain — “Did That Really Happen? How Our Memories Betray Us”

The research behind the reason the recap email exists. Most people believe memory works like a camera; it does not, and the way a question is worded changes what a witness later remembers seeing. Half an hour, clear American English, full transcript on the page.

Tip: listen once without the transcript, then read it and mark every sentence where the host reports what a researcher said. That is the whole grammar of this lesson, used for real.

Listen on NPR ↗
Talk
Celeste Headlee — “10 Ways to Have a Better Conversation” (TED)

A radio interviewer on listening as a skill rather than a courtesy, including the rule this lesson depends on: if you are building your answer while the other person is talking, you did not hear the sentence you are about to report. Eleven minutes, and she speaks fast.

Tip: watch it once with subtitles and once without, and note which of her ten rules you break in English but not in Portuguese. That difference is nerves, not language.

Lesson 10 — Precision at the Table

Podcast
Acquired — “Due Diligence”

Two investors walking through exactly what a buyer checks, in what order, and which founder answers make them slow down. It is the other side of the table talking openly, and the whole episode is a list of the questions this lesson taught you to answer before they are asked.

Steven Pinker — “The Sense of Style” (Talks at Google)

The shorter, faster, American-audience version of the same argument, with more examples of real sentences rewritten in front of you. If the hour-long talk is too much, start here: it is under an hour and the pace suits a second listen at full speed.

Gramática em português

A mesma gramática do Grammar in Context do Pre-class, explicada em português e com exemplo. Toque na aula para abrir. A mesma explicação também aparece no Pre-class, logo abaixo do texto do Grammar in Context.

Por que esta aba existe. Você pediu: “uma explicação em português mesmo, com exemplo”. Cada aula, da 1 em diante, ganha aqui um quadro com o que é, quando usar, como se monta e o erro mais comum.
Lesson 01 -- Gramática em português

Present simple e o -s da terceira pessoa (falar da empresa no presente)

Explicação em português de Present simple e o -s da terceira pessoa, no contexto de falar da empresa no presente. Toque para abrir.
▼

1. O que é. É o tempo verbal do que é verdade sempre, do que a empresa faz e de como as coisas funcionam: “We specialize in data” (a gente é especialista em dados), “Revenue comes from consulting” (a receita vem de consultoria). Em português o verbo muda para cada pessoa (eu faço, ele faz, nós fazemos). Em inglês ele quase não muda: a única mudança é um -s quando o sujeito é he, she ou it.

2. Quando usar. Para apresentar a Dataside, explicar o que vocês fazem, de onde vem o dinheiro e como o comprador trabalha. É o tempo da primeira reunião. E é onde o -s faltando mais aparece, porque você fala da empresa o tempo todo.

3. A regra em uma frase. Sujeito he, she, it (ou qualquer coisa que seja uma só: uma empresa, a receita, o comprador) leva -s no verbo. Todo o resto fica sem nada.

4. Quem leva -s e quem não leva

SujeitoVerboExemploEm português
I, you, we, theysem nadaWe specialize in data and AI.A gente é especialista em dados e IA.
he, she, itcom -sShe wants a faster close.Ela quer fechar mais rápido.
uma empresa (= it)com -sDataside specializes in data.A Dataside é especialista em dados.
uma coisa (= it)com -sMost of our revenue comes from consulting.A maior parte da nossa receita vem de consultoria.
uma pessoa (= he / she)com -sThe buyer wants three years of numbers.O comprador quer três anos de números.
várias pessoas (= they)sem nadaOur engineers work inside the client company.Nossos engenheiros trabalham dentro da empresa do cliente.

O truque: antes de falar, pergunte “o sujeito é uma coisa só?”. Se for, o verbo leva -s. Dataside, revenue, the firm, the market: tudo isso é it.

5. Como escrever o -s

Quase sempre é só acrescentar -s: work → works, want → wants, run → runs.

Termina em -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: acrescenta -es. focus → focuses, finish → finishes, go → goes, do → does.

Termina em consoante + y: troca por -ies. specify → specifies, try → tries.

Irregular: have → has. Dataside has three hundred people. (A Dataside tem trezentas pessoas.)

6. Na negativa e na pergunta, o -s muda de lugar

TipoComo ficaExemploEm português
Afirmativaverbo + -sHe moves on price.Ele cede no preço.
Negativadoes not + verbo sem nadaThe buyer does not move on price.O comprador não cede no preço.
PerguntaDoes + sujeito + verbo sem nadaDoes the buyer need more time?O comprador precisa de mais tempo?
Com I / we / theydo not / DoWe do not sell software. Do they want the data?A gente não vende software. Eles querem os dados?

O -s vai para o does e sai do verbo principal. Nunca nos dois lugares ao mesmo tempo.

7. Onde o português atrapalha

A empresa não parece uma pessoa. Em português “a Dataside é especialista” soa natural e você não pensa em pessoa nenhuma. Em inglês a empresa é um it, então leva -s igual a he e she.

Depender DE vira depender ON. Em português é “depende de”. Em inglês é it depends on. It depends on the valuation. (Depende do valuation.)

8. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Em vez deDigaPor quê
Dataside specialize in dataDataside specializes in dataEmpresa é it: leva -s.
The buyer want a faster closeThe buyer wants a faster closeO comprador é uma pessoa só.
She does not wantsShe does not wantO -s já está no does.
Does he needs more time?Does he need more time?Mesma coisa na pergunta.
It depends of the valuationIt depends on the valuationEm inglês é on.

9. O texto do Pre-class, trecho a trecho

O mesmo texto do Grammar in Context da Lesson 01, dividido em partes. Leia o inglês primeiro e só depois confira o português.

A buyer in New York asks a founder what his company does, and the founder answers well: the numbers are right, the story is clear, the strategy holds. And still, something in the room moves half a step back. Later nobody can say exactly what it was. It was one letter. Dataside specialize in data, he said. The buyer want a faster close. Three or four times in ten minutes, and each time the sentence arrived a little less finished than the thought behind it.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Um comprador em Nova York pergunta a um fundador o que a empresa dele faz, e o fundador responde bem: os números estão certos, a história está clara, a estratégia se sustenta. E mesmo assim alguma coisa na sala dá meio passo para trás. Depois ninguém consegue dizer exatamente o que foi. Foi uma letra. Dataside specialize in data, ele disse. The buyer want a faster close. Três ou quatro vezes em dez minutos, e a cada vez a frase chegava um pouco menos acabada do que o pensamento por trás dela.

English marks one person in the present simple, and only one. When the subject is he, she or it, the verb carries an -s: she wants, he runs, it costs. Everybody else takes the bare verb: I run, we specialize, they want.

EM PORTUGUÊS
O inglês marca uma pessoa só no present simple, e só uma. Quando o sujeito é he, she ou it, o verbo leva um -s: she wants (ela quer), he runs (ele administra), it costs (custa). Todos os outros usam o verbo puro: I run, we specialize, they want.

The trap for a Portuguese speaker is not the rule: the rule is simple and most speakers can recite it. The trap is the subject that does not look like a person. Dataside has three hundred people, because a company is an it. Revenue comes from consulting, because revenue is an it too. The private equity firm wants three years of numbers. Every one of those subjects is a single thing, and every one of them takes the -s.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A armadilha para quem fala português não é a regra: a regra é simples e a maioria sabe recitar. A armadilha é o sujeito que não parece uma pessoa. Dataside has three hundred people (a Dataside tem trezentas pessoas), porque empresa é it. Revenue comes from consulting (a receita vem de consultoria), porque receita também é it. The private equity firm wants three years of numbers (o fundo quer três anos de números). Cada um desses sujeitos é uma coisa só, e cada um leva o -s.

In the negative and in questions the -s moves house. It leaves the main verb and goes to do: he does not move on price, and does the buyer need more time? Saying she does not wants puts it in both places, which is the second most common version of the same mistake.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Na negativa e na pergunta, o -s muda de casa. Ele sai do verbo principal e vai para o do: he does not move on price (ele não cede no preço), e does the buyer need more time? (o comprador precisa de mais tempo?). Dizer she does not wants coloca o -s nos dois lugares, que é a segunda versão mais comum do mesmo erro.

And there is a habit that travels from Portuguese with it: depends of instead of it depends on. Neither one changes what a founder means. Both change how finished the founder sounds, and in a first meeting that is the only thing a buyer has to go on.

EM PORTUGUÊS
E tem um hábito que vem do português junto: depends of em vez de it depends on. Nenhum dos dois muda o que o fundador quer dizer. Os dois mudam o quanto ele soa acabado, e numa primeira reunião essa é a única coisa que o comprador tem para avaliar.

10. Teste rápido (toque para ver a resposta)

a) Dataside ___ (specialize) in data and artificial intelligence.

specializes: Dataside é uma empresa, então é it.

b) Most of our revenue ___ (come) from consulting.

comes: revenue é uma coisa só.

c) The buyer ___ move on price before due diligence. (negativa)

does not: e o verbo move fica sem -s.

d) It ___ the valuation. (depender de)

depends on.

Lesson 02 -- Gramática em português

Present perfect x past simple, com for e since (contar a história da empresa)

Explicação em português de Present perfect x past simple, com for e since, no contexto de contar a história da empresa. Toque para abrir.
▼

1. O que é. São dois jeitos de falar do passado. O past simple (we opened) conta um fato com data, que já fechou. O present perfect (we have opened) fala de algo que começou no passado e ainda conta hoje, sem dizer quando. Em português a gente usa o mesmo “abrimos” para as duas coisas; em inglês são duas formas diferentes.

2. Quando usar. Quando o comprador pergunta o que a empresa já fez: histórico, número de projetos, há quanto tempo vocês existem. Tudo o que é “até hoje” vai para o present perfect. Tudo o que tem ano, mês ou “last year” vai para o past simple.

3. A regra em uma frase. Disse quando, a frase fecha (past simple). Não disse quando, a conta continua (present perfect: have / has + particípio).

4. As duas formas lado a lado

FormaComo montaExemploEm português
Past simpleverbo no passadoWe opened our second office in 2018.Abrimos o segundo escritório em 2018.
Present perfecthave / has + particípioWe have delivered more than four hundred projects.Já entregamos mais de quatrocentos projetos (e a conta continua).
Present perfect (negativa)have never + particípioWe have never lost a client to a competitor.Nunca perdemos um cliente para um concorrente.
Present perfect (com it)has + particípioDataside has grown every year.A Dataside cresceu todo ano.

5. Palavras que escolhem a forma por você

Com past simple (fecha)Com present perfect (continua)
in 2018, last year, in March, two years ago, yesterdayfor, since, ever, never, already, so far, this year
We hired him last year.
Contratamos ele ano passado.		We have hired forty people so far.
Até agora contratamos quarenta pessoas.

6. For e since: os dois pedem present perfect

PalavraVem antes deExemploEm português
foruma duração (quanto tempo)Dataside has been in the market for fifteen years.A Dataside está no mercado há quinze anos.
sinceum ponto de partida (desde quando)I have been the CEO since 2009.Sou CEO desde 2009.

O português usa o presente (“sou CEO desde 2009”, “estamos aqui há quinze anos”). O inglês não aceita: com for e since é sempre have / has + particípio.

7. Onde o português atrapalha

“Sou CEO desde 2009” traduzido palavra por palavra vira I am CEO since 2009, que está errado. O certo é I have been CEO since 2009.

Data junto com present perfect. “Ano passado abrimos um escritório”: tem data, então é past simple. Last year we opened an office. Nunca last year we have opened.

A empresa continua sendo it. Então é has, não have: Dataside has grown.

8. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Em vez deDigaPor quê
I am CEO since 2009I have been CEO since 2009Com since é present perfect.
Last year we have opened an officeLast year we opened an officeTem data: a frase fecha.
Dataside have grownDataside has grownEmpresa é it: has.
We are in the market since fifteen yearsWe have been in the market for fifteen yearsQuinze anos é duração: for.

9. O texto do Pre-class, trecho a trecho

O mesmo texto do Grammar in Context da Lesson 02, dividido em partes. Leia o inglês primeiro e só depois confira o português.

There is a moment in every first meeting when a buyer stops asking what the company does and starts asking what it has done. The two questions sound similar and they are not. The first one can be answered by anybody with a website. The second one can only be answered by a company with a history, and English keeps a separate shape for it.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Existe um momento em toda primeira reunião em que o comprador para de perguntar o que a empresa faz e começa a perguntar o que ela já fez. As duas perguntas parecem iguais e não são. A primeira qualquer um com um site consegue responder. A segunda só uma empresa com história consegue responder, e o inglês tem uma forma separada para ela.

Dataside has been operating for fifteen years. We have delivered more than four hundred projects. We have never lost a client to a competitor. None of those three sentences carries a date, and that is the whole point.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Dataside has been operating for fifteen years (a Dataside opera há quinze anos). We have delivered more than four hundred projects (já entregamos mais de quatrocentos projetos). We have never lost a client to a competitor (nunca perdemos um cliente para um concorrente). Nenhuma dessas três frases tem data, e é exatamente essa a ideia.

The shape is have or has plus the past participle, and it does one job: it says the count is still running. Four hundred projects today, four hundred and one next month. Compare that with we opened our second office in 2018. The year is named, the sentence closes, and nothing about it can change. That is the past simple, and it is the right shape whenever the time is on the table.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A forma é have ou has mais o particípio, e ela faz uma coisa só: diz que a conta ainda está correndo. Quatrocentos projetos hoje, quatrocentos e um no mês que vem. Compare com we opened our second office in 2018 (abrimos o segundo escritório em 2018). O ano foi dito, a frase fecha, e nada nela pode mudar. Isso é o past simple, e é a forma certa sempre que o tempo está na mesa.

The rule underneath both is short enough to carry into a meeting: name the time and the sentence closes; leave the time out and you are still counting. With for and since the count is explicit (for takes a length of time, since takes a starting point) and both of them require the present perfect, always.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A regra por trás das duas é curta o bastante para levar para uma reunião: disse o tempo, a frase fecha; deixou o tempo de fora, você ainda está contando. Com for e since a conta fica explícita (for vem com uma duração, since com um ponto de partida) e os dois exigem o present perfect, sempre.

Two traps cost a Portuguese speaker the most, and they are both traps of translation rather than of grammar. The first is since with the simple present. In Portuguese the equivalent sentence sits comfortably in the present tense, so the direct translation arrives as I am CEO since 2009. English will not take it: it has to be I have been CEO since 2009.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Duas armadilhas custam mais caro para quem fala português, e as duas são de tradução, não de gramática. A primeira é since com o presente simples. Em português a frase equivalente fica confortável no presente (“sou CEO desde 2009”), então a tradução direta sai I am CEO since 2009. O inglês não aceita: tem que ser I have been CEO since 2009.

The second trap is a named time glued to a present perfect (Last year we have opened an office) and the fix is to drop back to the past simple: Last year we opened an office. And underneath both, the permanent one: a company is an it, so it takes has. Not Dataside have grown. Dataside has grown.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A segunda armadilha é um tempo com nome grudado num present perfect (Last year we have opened an office), e o conserto é voltar para o past simple: Last year we opened an office (ano passado abrimos um escritório). E por baixo das duas, o erro de sempre: empresa é it, então leva has. Não Dataside have grown, e sim Dataside has grown (a Dataside cresceu).

10. Teste rápido (toque para ver a resposta)

a) Dataside ___ (operate) for fifteen years.

has been operating: tem for e a empresa é it.

b) We ___ (deliver) more than four hundred projects.

have delivered: sem data, a conta continua.

c) We ___ (open) our second office in 2018.

opened: tem ano, a frase fecha.

d) I ___ the CEO since 2009.

have been: com since, present perfect.

e) We ___ (never / lose) a client to a competitor.

have never lost.

Lesson 03 -- Gramática em português

Present perfect continuous: have been + -ing (há quanto tempo algo vem acontecendo)

Explicação em português de Present perfect continuous: have been + -ing, no contexto de há quanto tempo algo vem acontecendo. Toque para abrir.
▼

1. O que é. É a forma que diz que uma atividade começou no passado e continua acontecendo agora: “We have been building the engine since 2022” (estamos construindo o motor desde 2022). Em português a gente diz isso com o presente (“estamos construindo desde 2022”, “faz seis semanas que eles fazem a due diligence”).

2. Quando usar. Quando a pergunta é há quanto tempo (how long): processos que não pararam, coisas em andamento numa due diligence. Se a pergunta é quantos (how many), você volta para o present perfect simples da aula 2.

3. A regra em uma frase. have / has + been + verbo com -ing, para atividade que ainda está em andamento.

4. Como monta

SujeitoFormaExemploEm português
I, you, we, theyhave been + -ingWe have been building the forecasting engine since 2022.Estamos construindo o motor de previsão desde 2022.
he, she, ithas been + -ingOur pipeline has been growing every quarter.Nosso pipeline vem crescendo todo trimestre.
theyhave been + -ingThey have been running due diligence for six weeks.Eles estão fazendo a due diligence há seis semanas.
PerguntaHow long has / have ... been + -ing?How long has the engine been in production?Há quanto tempo o motor está em produção?

5. Quantos ou há quanto tempo?

A pergunta é...FormaExemploEm português
how many? (um resultado contado)have + particípioWe have signed four new contracts this quarter.Assinamos quatro contratos novos neste trimestre.
how long? (uma atividade em andamento)have been + -ingWe have been signing contracts since March.Estamos fechando contratos desde março.

As duas frases podem ser verdade sobre os mesmos três meses. Uma mostra o resultado, a outra mostra o processo.

6. Verbos que não aceitam -ing

Alguns verbos descrevem um estado, não uma atividade, e por isso nunca ganham -ing: be, have (no sentido de ter, possuir), know, need, want, mean.

Com eles, use o present perfect simples:
I have known their head of corporate development for ten years. (Conheço o diretor de desenvolvimento corporativo deles há dez anos.)

E não I have been knowing him.

7. Onde o português atrapalha

Presente no lugar do perfect. “Fazemos isso há seis semanas” traduzido direto vira we are doing this since six weeks, errado duas vezes: no tempo verbal e na preposição. O certo é we have been doing this for six weeks.

For x since (igual à aula 2): for + duração (six weeks), since + ponto de partida (March, 2022).

Pipeline, empresa, mercado: tudo it. Então é has been, nunca have been.

8. Onde quase todo mundo escorrega

Em vez deDigaPor quê
We are doing this since six weeksWe have been doing this for six weeksTempo verbal e preposição.
I have been knowing him for ten yearsI have known him for ten yearsKnow é estado: sem -ing.
The pipeline have been growingThe pipeline has been growingPipeline é it.
How long the engine is in production?How long has the engine been in production?Pergunta de duração pede perfect.

9. O texto do Pre-class, trecho a trecho

O mesmo texto do Grammar in Context da Lesson 03, dividido em partes. Leia o inglês primeiro e só depois confira o português.

There is a question a serious buyer asks that a curious one never does. Not what do you do, and not even what have you done, but how long has it been running. The reason is not politeness. A result can be a lucky quarter; a process that has not stopped for two years is much harder to fake, and much harder to lose.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Existe uma pergunta que o comprador sério faz e o curioso nunca faz. Não o que vocês fazem, nem mesmo o que vocês já fizeram, mas how long has it been running (há quanto tempo isso está rodando). O motivo não é educação. Um resultado pode ser um trimestre de sorte; um processo que não parou em dois anos é muito mais difícil de fingir, e muito mais difícil de perder.

So the shape English uses for duration is the shape that fills a due diligence call: we have been building the engine since 2022, the pipeline has been growing every quarter since March, they have been running diligence for six weeks.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Por isso a forma que o inglês usa para duração é a forma que enche uma call de due diligence: we have been building the engine since 2022 (estamos construindo o motor desde 2022), the pipeline has been growing every quarter since March (o pipeline vem crescendo todo trimestre desde março), they have been running diligence for six weeks (eles estão fazendo a diligência há seis semanas).

The form is have or has plus been plus the -ing verb, and the test that chooses it is one question: can you answer how many, or only how long? We have signed four contracts answers how many, so it is the ordinary present perfect: a counted result. We have been signing contracts since March answers how long, so it is the continuous: an activity still under way.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A forma é have ou has mais been mais o verbo com -ing, e o teste que escolhe essa forma é uma pergunta só: você consegue responder quantos, ou só há quanto tempo? We have signed four contracts (assinamos quatro contratos) responde quantos, então é o present perfect comum: um resultado contado. We have been signing contracts since March (estamos fechando contratos desde março) responde há quanto tempo, então é o contínuo: uma atividade ainda em andamento.

Both are true about the same three months. They simply point at different things, and a buyer listens for which one you reach for first.

EM PORTUGUÊS
As duas são verdade sobre os mesmos três meses. Elas só apontam para coisas diferentes, e o comprador presta atenção em qual das duas você usa primeiro.

Two things trip a Portuguese speaker here. The first is that Portuguese covers this ground with the simple present tense, so the direct translation arrives as we are doing this since six weeks, which is wrong twice over: wrong tense and wrong preposition. It has to be we have been doing this for six weeks, with for before a length and since before a starting point.

EM PORTUGUÊS
Duas coisas derrubam quem fala português aqui. A primeira é que o português resolve isso com o presente simples (“fazemos isso há seis semanas”), então a tradução direta sai we are doing this since six weeks, que está errado duas vezes: tempo verbal errado e preposição errada. Tem que ser we have been doing this for six weeks, com for antes de uma duração e since antes de um ponto de partida.

The second is that some verbs refuse the -ing entirely because they describe a state rather than an activity: be, have in the sense of owning, know, need, want, mean. Not I have been knowing him for ten years. I have known him for ten years. And underneath all of it, the permanent one: the pipeline, the company and the market are each an it, so they take has, never have.

EM PORTUGUÊS
A segunda é que alguns verbos recusam o -ing completamente, porque descrevem um estado e não uma atividade: be, have no sentido de possuir, know, need, want, mean. Não I have been knowing him for ten years, e sim I have known him for ten years (conheço ele há dez anos). E por baixo de tudo, o erro de sempre: o pipeline, a empresa e o mercado são cada um it, então levam has, nunca have.

10. Teste rápido (toque para ver a resposta)

a) We ___ (build) the forecasting engine since 2022.

have been building: atividade que continua.

b) We ___ (sign) four new contracts this quarter.

have signed: é um número, responde “quantos”.

c) Our pipeline ___ (grow) every quarter.

has been growing: pipeline é it.

d) The acquirer has been running due diligence ___ six weeks.

for: seis semanas é duração.

e) I ___ (know) their head of corporate development for ten years.

have known: know não aceita -ing.

Lesson 04 -- Gramática em português

If + presente, will + verbo; unless (fazer propostas numa negociação)

Explicação em português de If + presente, will + verbo; unless, no contexto de fazer propostas numa negociação. Toque para abrir.
▼

1. O que é. É a frase de troca: “se você fizer X, a gente faz Y”. Em inglês: “If you move on the threshold, we will move on the timetable” (se vocês cederem na meta, a gente cede no cronograma). As duas metades falam do futuro, mas a metade do if fica no presente.

2. Quando usar. Em toda negociação, quando você quer trocar em vez de aceitar ou recusar. Também para estabelecer limites de um jeito que não soa como “não”: unless.

3. A regra em uma frase. If + presente, depois will + verbo puro. Nunca will depois de if.

4. As três frases de condição desta aula

FormaPara quêExemploEm português
If + presente, will + verbouma proposta, algo que ainda vai ser decididoIf you move on the threshold, we will move on the timetable.Se vocês cederem na meta, a gente cede no cronograma.
unless = if notum limite que soa como condiçãoWe will not sign anything unless the clause protects the team.Não assinamos nada a menos que a cláusula proteja o time.
If + presente, presenteuma regra já combinada, que acontece sozinhaIf revenue passes the threshold, the earnout pays in full.Se a receita passa da meta, o earnout paga integral.

A terceira não é proposta: é como uma cláusula de contrato. Use para o que já está acordado, nunca para o que ainda está negociando.

5. Por que o “se” fica no presente

Em português a gente usa o futuro do subjuntivo nas duas metades: “se você aceitar, a gente vai fechar”. A tradução direta põe will dos dois lados.

O inglês não aceita will depois de if. A metade do if fica no presente simples:
If you accept, we will close in June. (Se vocês aceitarem, fechamos em junho.)
E não if you will accept.

E o -s da aula 1 continua valendo depois do if: If the buyer accepts our number. (Se o comprador aceitar o nosso número.)

6. Palavras de contrato que andam com essas frases

PalavraO que éExemploEm português
